# Explanations

These pages explain how XC™ Circuit works and why it works that way. Read them when you want to understand what's going on; for step-by-step lessons see the [Tutorials](/tutorials/), and for every key and function the [API reference](/api/).

## Building bots

- **[Events, actions and values](./blocks-and-wires)**: the three kinds of blocks, and how a flow runs through them.
- **[Texts and `${…}`](./expressions)**: JavaScript in any text, and where the names in it come from.
- **[Projects and workspaces](./projects)**: what's in a project folder, and how to organize a bot.
- **[Variables and stored data](./data)**: values for one run, for a workspace, for the whole bot, and data that survives restarts.
- **[Try Zones and errors](./errors)**: what happens when something fails, and how to handle it.

## Behind the scenes

- **[Plugins](./plugins)**: everything is a plugin; the kinds of plugins and what each may do.
- **[Running and exporting](./running)**: how the editor runs your bot, and what an export contains.
- **[Tokens and safety](./safety)**: where secrets are kept, and why editor scripts are sandboxed.

<!-- docs/plugins/index.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/plugins/ -->

# Make a plugin

::: info In short
A plugin is a folder with a `plugin.toml`. Put it in a project's `plugins/` folder (or your own plugins folder), save a file, and XC™ Circuit loads it right away. Blocks run in the bot; an `editor.js` adds panels, commands and checks to the editor. Errors show in the Console and the Problems panel.
:::

This guide takes you from an empty folder to a plugin you can share. The [Reference](/api/) lists every key and function; the [Recipes](./recipes) show complete examples for common tasks; [Share and update](./share) covers packaging and versions.

## What can a plugin do?

| I want to… | Make | Runs in | Start with |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| add a **block** to the picker | a block file in `blocks/` | the bot | [Your first block](/tutorials/first-block) |
| add a **panel, command or check** to the editor | an `editor.js` | the editor (sandboxed) | [Your first editor plugin](/tutorials/first-editor-plugin) |
| make something **float over the editor** | an overlay in `editor.js` | the editor | [Desk Pet](https://github.com/XCraftTM/XC-Circuit/tree/main/examples/plugins/desk-pet) |
| change how the app **looks** | a theme | the editor | [Themes](/api/themes) |
| **translate** the app | a locale file | the editor | [Translate the app](/tutorials/translate) |
| offer **starter bots** in New Project | a template | the editor | [Templates](/api/templates) |
| add **settings** to Bot › Settings | a settings file | the editor and the bot | [Plugin settings](/api/build-modes#plugin-settings) |
| support another **chat app** | a build mode, runtime library and pin types | the bot | [Build modes](/api/build-modes) |

One plugin can do several of these: DemoBot's own plugin has blocks and an editor script.

## The folder

```
acme.tools/
├─ plugin.toml        what it is and what it adds
├─ blocks/
│  └─ shout.js        a block
├─ editor.js          panels, commands, checks
└─ icons/
   └─ acme.svg
```

```toml
id          = "acme.tools"
name        = "Acme Tools"
version     = "1.0.0"
author      = "Acme"
description = "A block and a panel for Acme bots."

[engines]
circuit = "^1.0"

[contributes]
blocks = ["blocks/*.js"]
icons  = ["icons/*.svg"]

[editor]
script = "editor.js"
```

Pick an `id` that's yours (`yourname.something`, lowercase) and start every block id and command id with it: two plugins can't use the same ids. Every key is in [plugin.toml](/api/plugin-toml).

## Where to keep it while you work

| Folder | Loaded | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the project's `plugins/` | only with that project | a plugin for one bot: it travels with the project (and its exports) |
| your plugins folder (Plugins › Open folder) | in every project | a plugin you use everywhere |
| a folder in `XC_CIRCUIT_PLUGINS` | in every project | developing a plugin in its own Git repository |

`XC_CIRCUIT_PLUGINS` is an environment variable with one or more folders (separated by `;` on Windows, `:` on Linux), each holding plugin folders. Start XC Circuit from a terminal that has it set:

```powershell
$env:XC_CIRCUIT_PLUGINS = "C:\code\my-plugins"; & "C:\Program Files\XC Circuit\xc-circuit.exe"
```

## The loop: save, look, fix

XC Circuit watches plugin files. **Save a file and it loads again**: a block file, the editor script, a theme, a translation. You don't restart anything:

- **Blocks** appear in the picker (search for their name). Blocks already on the canvas take the new shape; a running bot uses the new code after a restart (Save restarts it, if *Restart on save* is on).
- **Editor scripts** start again: their panels are drawn again, their commands are in the Plugins menu at once. Variables at the top of the script start over; what's in `xc.storage` and `xc.data` stays.
- **Themes and translations** apply right away.

The Plugins view in the side bar lists every plugin and whether its script runs. **Reload** there loads every plugin again, for a file the watcher missed.

## When something's wrong

| Where | What you see |
| --- | --- |
| **Problems** panel | a `plugin.toml` or block file that couldn't be read, a missing dependency, a block id used twice, problems your `xc.check` returns |
| **Console** | errors from commands, timers and events (with the file and line), what your blocks log with `ctx.log`, and a block that fails while the bot runs |
| the **panel** itself | an error in its `render`, above what it showed last |
| the **block** on the canvas | a block that failed turns red (the Console says why) |
| Plugins view | *Script · error*, with the reason |

An editor script that crashes is turned off until you save one of its files. One that takes too long (100 ms to draw, 1 s for a command) is stopped with an error saying so.

**Logging.** In blocks: `ctx.log.info("…", value)`. In editor scripts: `xc.log("…", value)`. Both go to the Console; objects are shown readably.

## TypeScript and your code editor

Blocks and editor scripts can be TypeScript (`.ts`): XC Circuit removes the types when it loads them. For completion and checking in your code editor, use the types in the repository's [`sdk/`](https://github.com/XCraftTM/XC-Circuit/tree/main/sdk) folder:

```ts
// a block
import { defineBlock } from "@xc-circuit/sdk";
export default defineBlock({ id: "acme.shout", kind: "value", /* … */ });
```

```js
// editor.js
/// <reference types="@xc-circuit/sdk/editor" />
xc.command({ id: "acme.hello", title: "Hello", run() { xc.log("Hi") } });
```

Split a bigger editor script into files with `require("./lib/util.js")` (`.js`, `.ts` or `.json`, only the plugin's own files). A block is one file.

## What's allowed where

| | Editor script (`editor.js`) | Block (in the bot) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Files, network, programs | no | yes (it's a Node.js program) |
| npm packages | no | yes: `requires.dependencies` and [`ctx.require`](/api/ctx#require) |
| The project | read, and change with undo | only its own values and what's wired in |
| Time | 100 ms to draw, 1 s for a command | as long as it needs |
| Asks before loading | no | no, so only use block plugins you trust |

Because editor scripts can't reach files or the network, they start without asking, even in a project you downloaded. Block code runs with the bot's full access, like any npm package: see [Tokens and safety](/explanations/safety).

## Next

- [Recipes](./recipes): complete examples to copy.
- [Share and update](./share): versions, zips, updates.
- [Reference](/api/): every key and function.

# API reference

Every key and function plugins can use. New here? Start with the [Plugin guide](/plugins/) (how to make, test and share a plugin, with [recipes](/plugins/recipes)) and the tutorials [Your first block](/tutorials/first-block) and [Your first editor plugin](/tutorials/first-editor-plugin).

## What do you want to do?

| I want to… | Read |
| --- | --- |
| make a **new block** for the picker | [Blocks](./blocks) → [Fields and types](./fields) → [Run context (ctx)](./ctx) |
| add a **panel, command or check** to the editor | [Editor plugins (xc)](./editor) → [Panels (ui)](./panels) |
| make something **float over the editor** (a desk pet) | [Overlays](./editor#xc-overlay) |
| support a **new kind of bot** (another chat app) | [Build modes](./build-modes) → [Runtime libraries](./runtime-libs) → [Pin types](./pin-types) |
| make a **theme** | [Themes](./themes) |
| **translate** the app | [Translations](./locales) |
| offer a **starter bot** in New Project | [Templates](./templates) |
| read or write **project files** with other tools | [Project format](./project-format) |

## Every plugin is a folder

```
my.plugin/
├─ plugin.toml   what it is, what it adds   → plugin.toml
├─ blocks/       blocks (.js, .ts)          → Blocks
├─ editor.js     panels, commands, checks   → Editor plugins
├─ modes/        kinds of bots (.toml)      → Build modes
├─ runtime/      code for a kind of bot     → Runtime libraries
├─ types/        value types (.toml)        → Pin types
├─ themes/       themes (.toml)             → Themes
├─ locales/      translations (.toml)       → Translations
├─ icons/        icons (.svg, .png)
└─ templates/    starter bots               → Templates
```

Only [`plugin.toml`](./plugin-toml) is required. Share a plugin as a `.zip` of its folder: people install it with **Plugins › Install from Zip…**

## Types for your code editor

The repository's [`sdk/`](https://github.com/XCraftTM/XC-Circuit/tree/main/sdk) folder is the `@xc-circuit/sdk` package:

```ts
import { defineBlock } from "@xc-circuit/sdk";        // blocks
/// <reference types="@xc-circuit/sdk/editor" />      // editor plugins (xc, ui)
```

## Versions

The plugin API is version **1.0**. A plugin says which versions it works with in `plugin.toml` (`[engines] circuit = "^1.0"`); plugins for another major version aren't loaded. Additions in 1.x keep old plugins working.

<!-- docs/download.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/download -->

# Download

::: info Early Access
XC™ Circuit is in Early Access: it works and is used for real bots, but expect rough edges. See the [known issues](/known-issues) and [what's new](/changelog). It's [built with AI assistance](/made-with-ai).
:::


## After downloading

- **Windows Setup**: run it. It installs for you only; no administrator needed.
- **Windows .zip** or **Linux .tar.gz**: unpack it anywhere and start `xc-circuit.exe` (Windows) or `xc-circuit` (Linux).
- **AppImage**: make it executable (right-click › Properties › *Allow executing*, or `chmod +x`), then double-click it.
- **.deb**: `sudo apt install ./XC-Circuit-…deb` · **.rpm**: `sudo dnf install ./XC-Circuit-…rpm`

Not sure whether your computer is x64 or ARM64? Almost every PC is x64; ARM64 is mostly laptops with a Snapdragon chip.

::: tip "Windows protected your PC"?
The installer isn't signed yet, so Windows asks first. Choose **More info › Run anyway**.
:::

## Updates

The app looks for newer versions itself (at start, and from Help › Check for Updates; you can turn the check off in Settings).

- **Installed with the Windows Setup, or an AppImage:** **Update and restart** downloads the new version, checks it against the checksum GitHub publishes, and installs it as XC Circuit closes (asking about unsaved changes first). Then XC Circuit opens again. On Windows only a small progress window shows; installed for everyone, Windows asks for administrator rights. When newer blocks are offered too, the same button updates them first, so one click does both.
- **.deb, .rpm, .zip or .tar.gz:** **Download** opens the release page; install the new file as you did the first one.

## What you need

- **Node.js 22 or newer** to run bots. The first start finds it, or installs it for you: with winget or the official installer on Windows, as a private copy on Linux.
- The npm packages a bot needs (discord.js for Discord bots, @fluxerjs/core for Fluxer bots) are installed once, on the first run, into `%APPDATA%\XC Circuit\packages` or `~/.local/share/xc-circuit/packages`.

## What's in the download

| File or folder | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `xc-circuit` / `xc-circuit.exe` | The editor, with the Node.js runtime that runs your block graphs built in |
| `plugins/` | The bundled plugins: Circuit Core, Discord Bot, Fluxer Bot and Server Tools |
| `examples/` | DemoBot and the starters New Project offers |
| `README.md` | A short guide to the editor |
| `LICENSE`, `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt`, `licenses/` | The licence and the licences of what's built in |

Your own plugins go into `%APPDATA%\XC Circuit\plugins` (Windows) or `~/.local/share/xc-circuit/plugins` (Linux); Plugins › Open folder opens it.

## From source

The code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/XCraftTM/XC-Circuit). With Rust installed:

```bash
cargo run -p circuit-editor
```

The first start opens `examples/DemoBot`. See the [licence](https://github.com/XCraftTM/XC-Circuit/blob/main/LICENSE) for what you may do with the code: you can fork it to propose changes (blocks, translations, fixes) as pull requests.

<!-- docs/performance.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/performance -->

# Performance

::: info In short
XC™ Circuit draws a typical bot in **about 1 ms per frame** and runs at **800–1,100 frames a second** on a gaming PC when nothing holds it back. Even a workspace of **1,600 blocks** stays smooth on a 120 Hz screen on an everyday computer. Frames only drop with **thousands of blocks in one workspace** or **hundreds of blocks on screen at once on a 4K window**. Bots run **75,000–200,000 blocks a second** once exported.
:::

The bundled starter bots have 3 to 8 blocks per workspace, and even large bots rarely have more than 100 in one. Everything below is about how far beyond that you can go.

## How it's measured

A screen shows a new picture (a frame) 60 or 120 times a second, so the app has **16.7 ms** (60 Hz) or **8.3 ms** (120 Hz) per frame. If a frame takes longer, the screen shows the previous picture again and movement stutters: frames drop.

Two kinds of measurements:

- **Real frame rates:** the whole app in its window, drawing with the graphics card, with a made-up project that it pans and zooms by itself. Vsync is off, so it draws as fast as it can instead of waiting for the screen.
- **Frame times:** what XC Circuit does on the processor for each frame (building the interface and turning it into triangles), timed without a window, so many more cases can be compared. The graphics card then only draws the triangles, which took it about 0.2 ms a frame in the real measurements.

The tables show the **95th percentile**: 19 out of 20 frames are at least this fast. They ran on two computers:

| | CPU | Graphics | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Desktop** | AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D (8 cores) | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 SUPER | A fast gaming PC, Windows 11 |
| **Everyday** | AMD EPYC 7763, 4 cores of a shared server | none | GitHub's standard Windows machine: about 2× slower, like an ordinary laptop |

🟢 smooth at 120 Hz · 🟡 smooth at 60 Hz · 🔴 drops frames

## Real frame rates

The desktop, a 1440×900 window, Vulkan. Each workspace was shown still, panned across and zoomed from 100% to 25% and back.

| Blocks in the workspace | Still | Panning | Zooming | Slowest frames (95%) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 25 | 1,045 FPS | 1,139 FPS | 374 FPS | 🟢 3.0 ms |
| 200 | 836 FPS | 801 FPS | 304 FPS | 🟢 4.9 ms |
| 800 | 493 FPS | 483 FPS | 234 FPS | 🟢 5.9 ms |
| 1,600 | 312 FPS | 308 FPS | 181 FPS | 🟢 7.4 ms |

**Without a graphics card** (drawing in software with Mesa's llvmpipe on Linux, 4 cores of an AMD EPYC 9V45 server), the same test still runs at about 42–67 FPS still or panning, and 34–51 FPS while zooming: usable, but noticeably less smooth.

Out of more than 10,000 frames on the desktop, only two took longer than 16.7 ms (single hiccups while zooming). Zooming costs the most, because every text is laid out again at its new size. Your screen still shows at most its own refresh rate (60, 144, 240 …); the rest is headroom.

## Blocks in one workspace

Frame times with a few blocks on screen (100% zoom) and the rest of the workspace off screen. Off-screen blocks cost a little: their layout is kept, and checked each frame for changes.

| Blocks in the workspace | Desktop | Everyday |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 25 | 🟢 0.9 ms | 🟢 1.7 ms |
| 200 | 🟢 1.0 ms | 🟢 2.0 ms |
| 400 | 🟢 1.5 ms | 🟢 2.7 ms |
| 800 | 🟢 1.7 ms | 🟢 4.1 ms |
| 1,600 | 🟢 3.3 ms | 🟢 8.2 ms |
| 3,200 | 🟢 6.4 ms | 🔴 18.5 ms |

An everyday computer stays smooth at 120 Hz up to about **1,600 blocks** in one workspace and drops frames at 3,200; the desktop handles 3,200 at 120 Hz. For very big bots, split them into several workspaces (the Call Workspace block runs one from another): other workspaces cost nothing.

## Blocks on screen at once

The window filled edge to edge with blocks, from 100% zoom down to 25% (the smallest). More pixels mean more blocks fit, so a 4K window (2560×1440 at 150%) shows the most.

| Window | Zoom | Blocks on screen | Desktop | Everyday |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1400×900 | 100% | 12 | 🟢 0.6 ms | 🟢 1.1 ms |
| 1400×900 | 50% | 48 | 🟢 2.3 ms | 🟢 4.2 ms |
| 1400×900 | 35% | 88 | 🟢 3.1 ms | 🟢 6.0 ms |
| 1400×900 | 25% | 165 | 🟢 6.4 ms | 🟡 12.7 ms |
| 4K | 100% | 35 | 🟢 2.0 ms | 🟢 4.1 ms |
| 4K | 50% | 126 | 🟢 7.3 ms | 🟡 14.6 ms |
| 4K | 35% | 260 | 🟡 9.6 ms | 🔴 22.8 ms |
| 4K | 25% | 459 | 🔴 19.5 ms | 🔴 44.2 ms |

On a normal-sized window frames never drop, even fully zoomed out. On a **4K window**, about **130–250 blocks on screen** is where an everyday computer starts to drop frames (450 for the desktop). Drawing that many blocks is the one thing that costs real time: each one is a small form with its own fields.

## Working on the canvas

A workspace of 400 blocks at 50% zoom: what moving around and editing cost compared with doing nothing.

| What you do | 1400×900, desktop | 1400×900, everyday | 4K, desktop | 4K, everyday |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nothing (idle) | 🟢 2.8 ms | 🟢 6.1 ms | 🟡 8.8 ms | 🔴 18.1 ms |
| Moving the pointer | 🟢 2.8 ms | 🟢 6.4 ms | 🟡 8.5 ms | 🔴 18.0 ms |
| Panning | 🟢 2.8 ms | 🟢 5.5 ms | 🟡 8.8 ms | 🔴 18.1 ms |
| Zooming | 🟢 5.0 ms | 🟡 9.6 ms | 🟡 10.2 ms | 🔴 22.2 ms |
| Dragging a block | 🟢 3.0 ms | 🟢 5.6 ms | 🟢 7.5 ms | 🔴 17.2 ms |

Panning and dragging cost no more than standing still. A 400-block workspace with 120 blocks on a 4K screen is the one case that isn't smooth on an everyday computer (just under 60 frames a second).

When nothing changes, XC Circuit doesn't redraw (at most once a second, while a plugin's script runs), so an idle window uses almost no processor time. While blocks glow after running, the canvas redraws about 30 times a second.

## Everyday tasks

| Task | Desktop | Everyday |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Load every plugin (205 blocks, compiled in QuickJS) | 81 ms | 125 ms |
| Open a project (any size; it loads its plugins too) | 84 ms | 128 ms |
| Open a workspace of 25 blocks for the first time | 1.8 ms | 3.8 ms |
| Open a workspace of 200 blocks for the first time | 12 ms | 27 ms |
| Open a workspace of 800 blocks for the first time | 78 ms | 168 ms |
| Open a workspace of 1,600 blocks for the first time | 266 ms | 530 ms |
| Open the block picker | 14 ms | 28 ms |
| Each letter typed into the picker's search | 3.3 ms | 7.2 ms |
| Paste 100 blocks | 0.2 ms | 0.3 ms |
| Undo that | under 0.1 ms | under 0.1 ms |
| Save a project of 1,600 blocks | 1.0 ms | 2.3 ms |
| Start a bot, until its first block ran | 54 ms | 108 ms |
| Export a bot of 800 blocks (without installing its packages) | 0.8 ms | 3.6 ms |

A workspace takes longer the first time it's opened because each block's shape is worked out (its `define()` runs) and its texts are laid out once; after that, switching to it is instant. Exporting with "install packages" also runs npm, which takes as long as the download.

## Running bots

The runtime that runs your bot, timed with 10,000 rounds of each case. **Run in the editor** reports every block to the editor as it starts and ends (that's how blocks glow and show their times); an **exported bot** skips that.

| Case | Run in the editor, desktop | Exported, desktop | Run in the editor, everyday | Exported, everyday |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Blocks (Set Variable with Math) | 94,000 a second | 202,000 a second | 19,000 a second | 74,000 a second |
| Stored data (Increase Stored Value) | 147,000 a second | 294,000 a second | 27,000 a second | 83,000 a second |
| Signals (Emit Signal → On Signal) | 66,000 a second | 156,000 a second | 15,000 a second | 52,000 a second |

A block takes 5–15 microseconds in an exported bot. Real bots spend almost all their time waiting for Discord or Fluxer (a reply takes 50–300 ms), so the blocks themselves are never what makes a bot slow. During these tests a bot used 50–150 MB of memory, most of it Node.js itself.

## If it gets slow

- **Split very big workspaces.** Thousands of blocks in one workspace cost a little each frame, other workspaces cost nothing. Use Call Workspace to run one from another.
- **Zoom in a bit on big screens.** Hundreds of blocks on a 4K screen are the most expensive thing to draw.
- **Check the graphics driver.** If no graphics card driver can be used, XC Circuit draws in software (it says so in the Console). On Linux that still gave 34–67 FPS above; Windows' software renderer was much slower on GitHub's screenless servers (about 2 FPS), though that says more about those servers than about a normal PC. Installing the graphics driver fixes it.
- **Older graphics cards** (such as a Radeon HD 5000) can't do DirectX 12 or Vulkan, so Windows offers its software renderer for them. When that happens, XC Circuit checks whether OpenGL can use the card, and if so starts again with OpenGL and keeps using it from then on (remembered in `graphics.txt` in its data folder; delete that file to let it choose again). **Settings › Window › Graphics** picks by hand from the next start: Automatic, OpenGL or Older OpenGL (the `XC_RENDERER` environment variable still works too: `auto`, `opengl`, `glow` or `software`).
- **Lighter drawing** (Settings › Window) is for older computers: tick each part to leave out, or All.
  - **No shadows**: windows, menus and blocks without a shadow.
  - **No fading**: menus, tooltips and panels appear and go at once.
  - **Still glows**: empty required fields and blocks that just ran glow without pulsing. A pulsing glow has the app draw itself 30 times a second for as long as it shows; still, an empty field costs nothing, and a block that just ran fades in a few steps.
  - **Simpler edges**: edges without their soft fringe. The canvas draws about 55–65% fewer triangles (30,200 → 11,000 at 100% zoom), which matters most when drawing in software or on an old graphics chip.
  - **All without a graphics card** (on to start with) leaves all of them out whenever the app draws in software, whatever is ticked.
- **The dotted background** is one repeated picture of a dot, so it costs next to nothing (it used to be a small circle per dot: up to 20,000 triangles and a third of a canvas frame).

## Run them yourself

The benchmarks are in the repository. With [Rust](https://rustup.rs) and Node.js installed:

```bash
cargo run --release -p circuit-editor -- --fps fps.json
```

```bash
cargo test --release -p circuit-editor bench_ -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1
```

```bash
node runtime/bench/runtime.js
```

The first opens XC Circuit for about a minute: it uses a made-up project and its own settings in a temporary folder, moves by itself (don't click into it) and closes when done, writing `fps.json`. The others print tables like the ones above and write `target/bench/*.json`. The **Benchmarks** workflow on GitHub runs all three on GitHub's Windows and Linux machines.

Measured with XC Circuit 0.1.0 in November 2026.

# How XC™ Circuit is made

**XC™ Circuit is designed and directed by XCraftTM and built with AI assistance (Anthropic's Claude).**

We think you should know that before you use it, so here's what that means.

## Who does what

- **XCraftTM** decides what XC Circuit is and does: which features it gets, how they should look and feel, what's good enough. Every feature is tried, and problems found by using the app are sent back until they're right.
- **Claude** (an AI) writes most of the code, the documentation and the bundled art and sounds (icons, the desk pet, the sound effects), following those decisions.

## What we do about quality

- **Tests:** more than a hundred automated tests for the editor and runtime run before every release, plus checks of the real interface rendered offscreen.
- **Open to read:** the [source code](https://github.com/XCraftTM/XC-Circuit) is public, so anyone can see how it works.
- **Real use:** bots are tested against real Discord and Fluxer servers before a release.
- **Maintained:** bugs are fixed and reported crashes looked at. Report anything with Help › Report a Bug.

## What it means for you

- Your bots, projects and plugins are **yours**. XC Circuit doesn't use AI while you build or run bots, and nothing you make is sent anywhere.
- XC Circuit has **no telemetry**. It only goes online to check for updates (you can turn that off) and when your bot runs.

If you'd rather not use software made this way, we understand. If you do use it, we'd love to hear what you build.


---

<!-- docs/tutorials/first-bot.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/tutorials/first-bot -->

# Your first bot

A Discord bot with a `/ping` command that answers **"Pong! 42 ms"**. About 15 minutes.

You need XC™ Circuit ([download](/download)) and a Discord server where you may add bots.

## 1. Make the bot in Discord

1. Open the [Discord Developer Portal](https://discord.com/developers/applications) › **New Application**, name it *Ping Bot*.
2. **Bot** › **Reset Token** › copy the token. It's a password: don't share it.
3. **OAuth2 › URL Generator**: tick **bot** and **applications.commands**, then **Send Messages**. Open the link at the bottom and add the bot to your server.

## 2. Create the project

**File › New Project…**

![The New Project window](/screens/new-project.png)

1. Pick **Discord Bot**.
2. Type a name.
3. Keep **Empty project** (the others are finished bots to learn from).
4. **Create**.

## 3. Paste the token

**Bot › Settings…**

![Bot settings](/screens/bot-settings.png)

1. Paste the token.
2. **Save and close**.

::: tip Safe
The token is kept in your computer's password store, never in the project folder.
:::

## 4. Make the `/ping` command

**Bot › Slash Commands…**

![The Slash Commands window](/screens/slash-commands.png)

1. **+ New command**.
2. Name `ping`, description *Checks that the bot answers*.
3. **Save and close**.

## 5. Add the blocks

Right-click the empty canvas (or press **Space**).

![The block picker](/screens/block-picker.png)

1. Type `slash`.
2. Click **Slash Command**.

Then add **Send Message** the same way, and connect them:

![The finished blocks](/screens/ping-blocks.png)

1. Set **Command** to `/ping`.
2. Drag from the green arrow on Slash Command to Send Message.
3. Drag from **Interaction** to **Interaction**: this tells Send Message what to answer.
4. Type the text:

```
Pong! ${Date.now() - interaction.createdTimestamp} ms
```

`${…}` is JavaScript: here, how long ago the command was used.

## 6. Run it

![The Run button](/screens/run.png)

1. **Run** (or **F5**). The first run installs discord.js, which takes a moment.

Type `/ping` in your server. The bot answers, and the blocks light up as they run.

::: details It doesn't answer?
- The Console says why, and the failing block turns red.
- No token: step 3. Bot not in the server: step 1.3.
- New command not showing yet: save with **Ctrl+S**, which restarts the bot.
:::

**Ctrl+S** saves. **Shift+F5** stops the bot.

Next: [Values and texts](./values-and-texts).

<!-- docs/tutorials/values-and-texts.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/tutorials/values-and-texts -->

# Values and texts

A `/count` command that remembers how often each person used it: **"You've counted 3 times, Alex!"**

Start from the bot of [Your first bot](./first-bot).

## 1. Add the command

- **Bot › Slash Commands…** › **+ New command**: `count`.
- In the Workspaces panel, **+** adds a workspace: call it *Count command*.

## 2. Build it

Add **Slash Command**, **Increase Stored Value** and **Send Message**, connected with green arrows, then:

![The Count command's blocks](/screens/count-blocks.png)

1. Connect **User** to **Target**: every person gets their own count.
2. Set **Key** to `counts`.
3. Connect **Value** to the text's `${value}` input. It appears by itself when you type `${value}` in the text.
4. The text:

```
You've counted ${value} times, ${user.username}!
```

Also connect **Interaction** to Send Message's **Interaction**, as before.

## 3. Try it

**F5**, then use `/count` a few times. The number keeps going up, also after restarting the bot. The **Stored Data** view (database icon on the left) shows what's saved.

::: tip Let the editor write it
Type `${` in any text: a list shows what earlier blocks give. Pick one and it's written for you, such as `${#2.value}`.
:::

## What's what

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Outputs** (right side of a block) | values a block gives |
| **Inputs** (left side) | values a block takes |
| **`${…}`** in a text | JavaScript; names from earlier blocks just work |
| **Stored values** | kept across restarts, per user, server, member, channel or bot |

More: [Texts and ${…}](/explanations/expressions) · [Variables and stored data](/explanations/data).

<!-- docs/tutorials/first-block.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/tutorials/first-block -->

# Your first block

A **Greeting** block that says "Good morning", "Good afternoon" or "Good evening". Blocks are small JavaScript files.

## 1. Make a plugin in your project

In your bot's folder, create these folders and files:

```
Ping Bot/
└─ plugins/
   └─ my.blocks/
      ├─ plugin.toml
      └─ blocks/
         └─ greeting.js
```

`plugin.toml`:

```toml
id      = "my.blocks"
name    = "My blocks"
version = "1.0.0"

[contributes]
blocks = ["blocks/*.js"]
```

## 2. Write the block

`blocks/greeting.js`:

```js
module.exports = {
  id: "my.greeting",
  kind: "value",
  info: { name: "Greeting", description: "Good morning, afternoon or evening.", author: "You", version: "1.0.0" },
  fields: { name: { type: "text" } },
  outputs: { text: { type: "text" } },
  run({ fields }) {
    const hour = new Date().getHours();
    const part = hour < 12 ? "morning" : hour < 18 ? "afternoon" : "evening";
    return { text: `Good ${part}, ${fields.name || "you"}!` };
  },
};
```

Save. XC Circuit loads it right away.

## 3. Use it

Right-click the canvas:

![The picker finds the new block](/screens/greeting-picker.png)

1. Type `greet`.
2. There it is. Click it, and connect its **Text** to a Send Message.

## How it works

| Key | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `kind: "value"` | gives a value when another block needs it (others: `"action"`, `"event"`) |
| `fields` | what you fill in on the block |
| `outputs` | what it gives |
| `run()` | gets the fields, returns the outputs |

::: details An action with two ways out
```js
module.exports = {
  id: "my.coin_flip",
  kind: "action",
  info: { name: "Coin Flip", description: "Heads or tails.", author: "You", version: "1.0.0" },
  flows: ["heads", "tails"],
  run({ ctx }) {
    return ctx.next(Math.random() < 0.5 ? "heads" : "tails");
  },
};
```
`flows` are the green outputs; `ctx.next()` picks one.
:::

Everything a block can have: [Blocks](/api/blocks).


---

<!-- docs/tutorials/first-editor-plugin.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/tutorials/first-editor-plugin -->

# Your first editor plugin

Editor plugins add things to XC Circuit itself: panels, commands, checks, even a [desk pet](https://github.com/XCraftTM/XC-Circuit/tree/main/examples/plugins/desk-pet). They're JavaScript too.

We'll make a **Block Counter**: a command and a panel.

## 1. The plugin

In your bot's folder: `plugins/block.counter/plugin.toml`

```toml
id      = "block.counter"
name    = "Block Counter"
version = "1.0.0"

[editor]
script = "editor.js"
```

## 2. The script

`plugins/block.counter/editor.js`:

```js
xc.command({
  id: "counter.total",
  title: "Count all blocks",
  run() {
    xc.log(`${xc.project().name} has ${xc.blocks().length} blocks`);
  },
});

xc.panel({
  id: "counts",
  title: "Block Counter",
  render(ui) {
    ui.heading("Blocks per workspace");
    for (const w of xc.workspaces()) {
      const count = Object.keys(xc.workspace(w.key).nodes).length;
      ui.row((ui) => {
        ui.text(w.name);
        ui.text(`${count} blocks`, { muted: true });
      });
    }
    ui.button("Count all blocks", () => xc.run("counter.total"), { primary: true });
  },
});
```

Save. It loads right away, and again every time you save.

## 3. Try it

Open the **Plugins** menu:

![The Plugins menu](/screens/plugins-menu.png)

1. Your command: writes to the Console.
2. Your panel: opens it.

![The panel](/screens/block-counter-panel.png)

1. Dock it anywhere, like any panel.

## What else `xc` can do

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `xc.check(fn)` | problems for the Problems panel |
| `xc.overlay({…})` | something floating over the editor (the desk pet) |
| `xc.every(ms, fn)` | timers |
| `xc.playSound(file)` | sounds |
| `xc.addBlock(…)`, `xc.select(…)` | change the canvas |
| `xc.on("save" \| "botEvent" \| "selection", fn)` | react to the app |

All of it: [Editor plugins (xc)](/api/editor) and [Panels (ui)](/api/panels).

# Translate the app

Add a language for XC Circuit's menus and windows. (Blocks stay in English, so projects look the same for everyone.)

## 1. Start

**Settings** (gear at the bottom left, or **Ctrl+,**) › **Appearance**:

![Settings › Appearance](/screens/translate.png)

1. **Create a translation…**, then give the language's code (`fr`) and name (*Français*).

A file opens with every text of the app.

## 2. Translate

```toml
[strings]
"Save and close" = "Enregistrer et fermer"
"{count} to fix" = "{count} à corriger"
"Run" = ""
```

- Keep `{words in braces}` as they are.
- Empty lines stay English: translate a bit at a time.

Save, and pick your language under **Interface language**. Changes show right away.

## 3. Share

It's a plugin folder: zip it and share it (others install it with **Plugins › Install from Zip…**), or send it to us as a pull request on [GitHub](https://github.com/XCraftTM/XC-Circuit).

More: [Translations](/api/locales).

<!-- docs/explanations/blocks-and-wires.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/blocks-and-wires -->

# Events, actions and values

A bot in XC™ Circuit is a graph of blocks connected by wires. Every block is one of three kinds, and the kind decides when it runs.

## The three kinds

| Kind | Chip | Runs… | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Event** | Event | when something happens: a command is used, a member joins, a timer fires | Slash Command, Member Joins, Every, On Start |
| **Action** | Action | when the flow reaches it, one after the other | Send Message, Add Role, If, Wait |
| **Value** | Value | where the flow reaches it, or when a block needs one of its outputs | Math, Join Text, Get Property |

An event **starts a flow**. The flow follows the green **action wires** from block to block: each action runs, finishes, and passes the flow on. Value blocks can go **in the flow** too: wire an Action into them and on out of them, and they run right there, once, and every block after them gets that result (a Random Number in the flow gives two later blocks the same number). That's the clearest way to read, say, a property of a command's option before using it. Left **to the side**, without Action wires, they're worked out when a block that's about to run needs their output, afresh each time.

```
[Slash Command] ──▶ [Get Stored Value]* ──▶ [Send Message]
                              ▲
                     [Math] ──┘  (values are worked out on demand)
```

## Two kinds of wires

- **Action wires** (green) connect an action output to an action input. They decide the order.
- **Value wires** connect an output, such as *User* or *Value*, to an input of the same or a compatible type. They carry data.

A value can come from any block that ran earlier in the same flow, or from a value block. The editor only lets you connect pins whose types fit (a *Member* can go where a *User* is needed, because a member converts to its user), and dragging a wire into empty canvas offers only the blocks that fit.

## One path per action output

An action output leads to one block; connecting it elsewhere replaces the old wire. Paths can join, but they only **branch** through blocks made for it: **If** (true/false), **Switch**, **For Each**, **Repeat**, or a block of your own with several [`flows`](/api/blocks#flows). This keeps the order of a flow obvious: you can always read it from left to right. A wire that would make an endless loop is refused.

## Several flows at once

Every event starts its own **run**. If two people use a command at the same time, two runs go through the same blocks independently, each with its own values and run variables. Blocks that wait (for Discord, a timer, the web) don't hold up other runs.

## Fields and pins

A block's **fields** are what you fill in on it: a text, a number, a choice. Most fields can also become a **pin**: click the faint pin next to the field (or *pin* in the Inspector) and connect a value to it instead. Some fields are pins only, because a fixed value makes no sense there (a member to give a role to, for example).

## Inputs the event fills in

An **Interaction** or **Server** input left unconnected takes the one of the event that started the flow (Slash Command, Button Pressed, Member Joined …), when that event gives one: the block says **from the event** instead of *connect*, and it isn't a problem. So Send Message replying to a command needs no wire for the interaction. Users, members, channels and messages are never filled in like this: an unconnected Ban or Delete Channel must not hit whoever started it, so connect those.

## Why it's built this way

- **Order you can see.** Bots are mostly "when X, do A, then B, then C". Action wires make that order visible and keep it unambiguous.
- **Values without wiring order.** Calculations don't need to be placed in the flow; they're worked out when used, so the flow stays short.
- **Plain JavaScript underneath.** Every block is a [JavaScript file](/api/blocks), and every text accepts [`${…}`](./expressions), so you can always drop down to code when a block doesn't exist yet.


---

<!-- docs/explanations/expressions.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/expressions -->

# Texts and `${…}`

Any text field (Send Message's text, Log, Join Text, the Embed and Layout Builders, …) can hold JavaScript inside `${…}`, exactly like a JavaScript template string:

```
Welcome ${member.displayName}! You're member #${server.memberCount}.
${xp >= 1000 ? "🏆 Veteran" : "🌱 Newcomer"}
It's ${new Date().getFullYear()}.
```

When the block runs, every `${…}` is evaluated and replaced by its result.

## Where names come from

A name inside `${…}` is looked up, in this order, in:

1. **The block's own fields**, by their key.
2. **The event's outputs**: `user`, `member`, `interaction`, `message`, … whatever the event that started the run gives.
3. **Run variables** set with Set Variable.
4. **Outputs of earlier blocks** on the same action path.

A name none of these give gets an **input of its own** under the text, so you can connect a value to it. Type `${ping}` and an input called *ping* appears.

## Values of a particular block

`#4` means block #4 (the number in its title bar), so `${#4.message.url}` is the *Message* output of block #4. Use this when several earlier blocks give an output with the same name, or when you want to be explicit. Typing `${` in a text lists the blocks before this one and their values; the editor writes the reference for you.

## Members of values

Values are real objects: a Discord *User* is a discord.js `User`, a *Member* a `GuildMember`. Their properties and reading methods work: `${user.username}`, `${member.roles.highest.name}`, `${user.displayAvatarURL()}`. Typing a `.` after a value inside `${…}` lists its members with their types, like a code editor. Collections (a server's `members.cache`, a member's `roles.cache`) list their own: `size`, `first()`, `get(id)`, `find(…)`, `filter(…)` …, and after one that gives back an item, the item's: `${server.members.cache.get(user.id).displayName}`, `${member.roles.cache.first().name}`. A Map lists `size`, `get(…)` and `has(…)`.

Blocks never give Collections: what a block puts out is a list of the items (a Collection a block's JavaScript returns becomes one too), so List Tools, For Each and the rest get the items. Inside `${…}` a Collection stays one, with the members above. To turn one into a list (in a field for any value, such as `${message.mentions.users}`), use **Collection to List**, which can also give the ids (keys) or both.

## Mentions

A user, member, role or channel in a text is a mention: `Welcome ${user}!` pings them, `${role}` pings the role and `${channel}` links the channel, as `<@id>`, `<@&id>` and `<#id>` do. For a name without a ping, use `${user.username}`, `${member.displayName}` or `${role.name}`. The list after `${` says which values ping (**pings them**) or link (**links it**). The **Mention** block does the same for an id, a list of people, `@everyone` or `@here`; Send Message's **Who gets pinged** decides who is notified.

## Splitting text

**Split Text** takes a text apart at a separator (spaces when it's empty, or `,`, `|` …) and gives the parts ready to use: **First**, **Last**, **Part** (by number: 1 is the first, -1 the last), **Rest** (everything after the first part) and **Count**. For `!kick @ada being rude`: First is `!kick`, Part 2 is `@ada`, Rest is `@ada being rude`.

## Dates and times

- **Date & Time**: now (or a given date), moved with **Add** (`1d 2h`, `30m`, `-1w`), as text: your own pattern such as `DD.MM.YYYY HH:mm` in a time zone such as `Europe/Berlin`, or a Discord timestamp that each reader sees in their own time zone and language.
- **Read Date**: what people type, as a date: `2026-12-24 18:00`, `24.12.2026`, `18:30`, `tomorrow 9:00`, `in 2h`, `1d 12h`, a unix time or a Discord timestamp. **Valid** says whether it could be read.
- **Time Between**: the time between two dates (empty is now) in days, hours, minutes and seconds, and as text such as `2 d 3 h`. A user or member counts from when the account was made.

## Errors

A mistake in an expression (a typo, reading a property of nothing) stops the block with an error that quotes the expression. Use optional chaining and fallbacks where a value may be missing: `${member?.nickname ?? user.username}`.

## Why JavaScript

Template strings are the JavaScript most people already know, they work for everything from a name to a calculation, and they run exactly as written: there's no separate formula language to learn, and anything you find in discord.js's documentation can be used directly.

::: details Older projects
Projects from before `${…}` used `{name}`. They are changed to `${name}` when the project opens.
:::


---

<!-- docs/explanations/projects.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/projects -->

# Projects and workspaces

## A project is a folder

```
My Bot/
├─ circuit.project.json    the project: name, build mode, shared settings
├─ commands/
│  └─ rank.json            one file per slash command
├─ workspaces/
│  ├─ welcome.json         one file per workspace
│  └─ rank-command.json
└─ plugins/                optional: plugins that belong to this project
   └─ my.blocks/
```

Everything is plain, formatted JSON, so a project works well in Git: changes show as readable diffs, and two people can work on different workspaces without conflicts. The exact format is in [Project format](/api/project-format).

What's **not** shared: the bot token and other secrets (they're in the [credential store](./safety)), and what belongs to your computer alone, such as the server the bot is uploaded to, where its databases are and its stored data. Those are kept in a hidden `.circuit/` folder that stays out of Git.

## Build modes

Each project has a **build mode**, chosen in File › New Project: *Discord Bot* (discord.js) or *Fluxer Bot* (fluxer.js). The mode decides which blocks the picker offers, the categories they're sorted into, the settings in Bot › Settings, and which npm packages the bot needs. Build modes come from plugins; see [Build modes](/api/build-modes).

## Workspaces

A workspace is one canvas. A bot can have any number, sorted into folders in the Workspaces panel. They all run together: splitting a bot into workspaces is only for you.

Good habits:

- **One workspace per command or feature**: *Rank command*, *Welcome*, *Moderation*.
- **Reuse with Call.** A *When Called* event in one workspace and *Call* blocks elsewhere make a flow you can use from many places, like a function. *Return* gives a value back.
- **Signals** (Emit Signal and On Signal) let one part of the bot tell others that something happened, without waiting for them.
- **Notes** explain a part of a workspace: *Add note* in the canvas toolbar, or *Note* above selected blocks to frame them. A note has a title, a description and a colour (the pencil button, or double-click its title). Drag its title to move it with the blocks inside (hold Alt to move only the note), and its edges or corners to resize it. Notes are selected, copied, pasted, duplicated and deleted like blocks: click the title, or draw a box around the whole note.

## Starters and examples

File › New Project can start from a working bot (welcome and auto role, moderation, levels, tickets, role menus; for Fluxer: basic commands, moderation). They are ordinary projects copied into your new folder; plugins can add their own (see [Templates](/api/templates)). Help › Open Example opens DemoBot.

## Safety nets

- **Undo/redo** per workspace (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y).
- **Backups**: every save keeps a snapshot outside the project (the newest 20, plus one a day for 14 days). File › Restore from backup… compares them with now and restores the whole project or one workspace.
- **Crash recovery**: unsaved changes are copied every 30 seconds (Settings › Backups changes how often) and offered back after a crash.


---

<!-- docs/explanations/data.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/data -->

# Variables and stored data

Bots need to remember things: for a moment, while a command runs, or for months. XC™ Circuit has two tools for that.

## Variables: while the bot runs

Variables are set with **Set Variable** and read with **Get Variable** (or by name in [`${…}`](./expressions)). They live in memory and come in three scopes:

| Scope | Lives for | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Run** | one run, from its event to its end | a value you work out early and need later in the same flow |
| **Workspace** | as long as the bot runs, shared by the runs of one workspace | a cache, a queue for one feature |
| **Global** | as long as the bot runs, shared by everything | state the whole bot needs |

Variables are gone when the bot stops.

## Stored data: across restarts

**Set, Get, Increase and Delete Stored Value**, **List Stored Keys** and **Leaderboard** keep data in a file, so it survives restarts. Each value has a **key** (such as `xp`) and belongs to a scope:

| Scope | One value per… |
| --- | --- |
| Whole bot | bot |
| Server | server |
| User | user, in every server |
| Member | user in one server |
| Channel | channel |

So `xp` for *Member* gives everyone their own XP in each server, while `xp` for *User* follows a person across servers.

The data is kept in `store.json`: in the project's `.circuit/data/` folder while the bot runs from the editor, and in `data/` next to an exported bot. While you work in the editor, the **Stored Data** view in the side bar shows it.

## Backups of bot data

A bot backs up its stored data when it starts and every 6 hours, keeping the newest 10 in a `backups` folder next to `store.json`. If the data is empty or damaged at start, the bot asks whether to restore a backup or start empty (a dialog in XC Circuit, a question in the terminal for exported bots).

## Timers: later, once

**Schedule** runs the **On Scheduled** blocks with the same name once, after a while (`30s`, `10m`, `1h 30m`, `3d`) or at a time (`2026-12-24 18:00`), with a **value** along: a text, or an object with what's needed later (`{ user, channel, text }`). For reminders, temporary bans, giveaways that end, a message that goes out on a day.

Timers are kept with the stored data, so they still run after the bot restarts. One that was due while the bot was off runs when it starts again, with **Late** saying by how much; turn off *Run missed ones* on On Scheduled to drop those instead. Users, channels and messages in the value come back as their data (id, name …), not as live objects: find the member again with its id when you need more.

- A **key** replaces an earlier timer with the same key: `remind-${user.id}` gives everyone one reminder at most.
- **Cancel Scheduled** removes timers before they run: by the id Schedule gave, by key, or all with a name.
- **List Scheduled** gives the waiting timers, soonest first.

**Every** is for things that repeat (every 10 minutes, every day at 9:00); it doesn't need saving.

## Files

The blocks in **Files** keep files in the bot's **files folder**: `.circuit/data/files` in the project while it runs from XC Circuit, `data/files` next to an exported bot. Paths are inside it (`notes.txt`, `tickets/123.json`); paths outside it are refused, so a bot can't touch the rest of the computer.

| Block | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Read File** | As text, JSON, a table (CSV: a list of rows, by the first line's column names), lines, or bytes. A missing file gives nothing (or an error, if you like). |
| **Write File** | Text, JSON, a table or bytes (a Build Canvas picture); replaces the file, or adds to its end (added text gets a line of its own; added rows no second header). |
| **List Files** | A folder's files, newest first, matching a name like `*.png`. |
| **File Action** | Checks that a file is there, deletes, copies or moves it, makes a folder. |
| **Download File** | Saves a file from the web, or a message's attachment (at most 25 MB unless you say otherwise). An address that comes from `${…}` or a wire (one people type) may only go to the public web; *Private addresses too* lifts that for addresses only you choose. |

Each gives the file's whole **path** on disk, which Send Message's **Files** takes.

## In a database

Stored values can be kept in MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite or MongoDB instead of `store.json`, and the database blocks read and write your own tables there. See [Databases](./databases).

## In your own blocks

Blocks reach the same data through [`ctx.vars`](/api/ctx#vars) and [`ctx.store`](/api/ctx#store), so a custom block and the built-in ones share it.


---

<!-- docs/explanations/databases.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/databases -->

# Databases

::: info In short
Add a database in **Bot › Settings › Databases** (MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite or MongoDB), then read and write it with **Get Rows**, **Insert Row**, **Update Rows**, **Delete Rows** and **SQL Query**. Stored values can live there too.
:::

[Stored data](./data) is enough for most bots. A database is worth it when the data gets big, when another program (a website, a dashboard) reads it too, or when you have one already.

## Adding a database

**Bot › Settings › Databases › + Add database**, then:

| Kind | What it needs |
| --- | --- |
| **MariaDB / MySQL**, **PostgreSQL** | Host, port, user, password and the database's name. Turn on SSL/TLS for databases on the internet. |
| **SQLite** | Only a file name, such as `bot.sqlite`: it's made in the bot's data folder the first time. Nothing to install. |
| **MongoDB** | Host and port, or a connection URL such as the `mongodb+srv://…` MongoDB Atlas gives. |

Instead of host, port, user and password, any kind can take a **connection URL**: `mysql://user:password@host:3306/name`, `postgres://…`, `mongodb+srv://…`.

**Test connection** connects the way the bot will and shows the server's version and its tables, or what went wrong: a wrong password, a host that isn't found, a port nothing answers on.

Passwords and connection URLs are kept in the system's password store, like the bot token, never in the project. The rest (host, user, database name) is in the project.

### The default database

One database is the **default**. Every database block has a **Database** list: *Default database*, or one by name. Blocks left on Default all switch when you choose another default, so a bot can move from a test database to the real one in one place.

### A database given on the block

**Database** can also be *Given here*: the block connects to a MariaDB / MySQL, PostgreSQL or MongoDB server it's given, such as one from a slash command's options. Kind, host, port, user, database name and SSL are fields you can type or connect; the **password** and the **connection URL** (which holds one) can only be connected: typed into a block they'd be saved in the project file.

This is off until you allow it: Bot › Settings › Databases › Safety › *Allow databases given on blocks*. Anyone who can use such a command can make the bot connect where they say (to machines on your own network, too), so only turn it on for commands you trust them with.

The bot keeps up to 8 given connections open for the next run with the same details, and closes the one used longest ago after that. An export gets the npm package of each kind chosen on a block.

## The blocks

| Block | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Get Rows** | The rows of a table that match the conditions: all of them (`rows`), the first one, and how many. In the Inspector: sort, at most, skip (for pages). |
| **Insert Row** | Adds a row. Gives the new row's id (an auto-increment column, or MongoDB's `_id`). |
| **Update Rows** | Changes columns of the rows that match. Gives how many. |
| **Delete Rows** | Deletes the rows that match. Gives how many. |
| **SQL Query** | Runs your own SQL (not MongoDB). |

**Conditions** are a column, a comparison (*is*, *is not*, *is more than*, *contains*, *starts with*, *is empty* …) and a value; a row has to match all of them (or, in the Inspector, any one). The number on the block says how many there are.

Update Rows and Delete Rows without any condition would change or delete every row, so they refuse unless **Every row without conditions** is turned on in the Inspector.

A user, channel or server given as a value counts as its **id**. Lists and objects are kept as JSON (in MongoDB, as they are). Keep Discord ids in text columns (`VARCHAR`, `TEXT`): they're too big for exact numbers in some databases.

In MongoDB, a *table* is a collection and a *column* is a field.

### SQL Query and `${…}`

```sql
SELECT xp, level FROM levels WHERE user_id = ${user.id} AND guild_id = ${server.id}
```

Each `${…}` is sent to the database as a **value**, separately from the SQL. So whatever people type into a command can't change the query (no SQL injection), and quotes need no escaping. That's also why `${…}` can't be a table or column name.

The tables have to exist before the bot uses them; SQL Query can make them:

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS levels (user_id VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY, xp INTEGER DEFAULT 0)
```

## Stored values in a database

**Keep stored values in** (on the same page) moves Set Stored Value, Get Stored Value, Increase, Leaderboard and the rest into a database, in a table `xc_store` the bot makes. The blocks don't change.

The first time, the bot copies what's in `store.json` into the database (when its table is still empty); `store.json` stays as it was. The Stored Data view shows and changes the values there, and each database's tables too. Backups of stored data are for `store.json` only: back up a database with its own tools.

## Exported bots

An export gets the database's npm package (`mysql2`, `pg` or `mongodb`) in its `package.json`. Passwords and URLs go to `.env`, as `XC_SECRET_DB_<ID>_PASSWORD` and `XC_SECRET_DB_<ID>_URL` (with *Include the bot token and secrets*); the id is the database's, such as `DB1`. A SQLite file is in the export's `data/` folder.

## In your own blocks

[`ctx.db()`](/api/ctx#db) is the same connection the built-in blocks use.


---

<!-- docs/explanations/canvas.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/canvas -->

# Pictures with Build Canvas

::: info In short
**Build Canvas** draws a picture (a welcome card, a rank card, a profile) from a design you make in the **Canvas Builder**. Connect its **File** to Send Message's **Files**.
:::

## The Canvas Builder

Add **Build Canvas** (in *Embeds & Layouts*) and press **Edit canvas…** on it, or **Open Canvas Builder** in the Inspector.

- **Start from** a Rank card, Welcome card or Profile card, or start empty.
- **Size** in pixels, with common sizes to pick from, and a **background** colour (or see-through).
- **Layers**, drawn bottom to top:

| Layer | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Shape** | A rectangle, with round corners if you like. |
| **Circle** | A circle or an ellipse. |
| **Picture** | From a web address, a file, or `${…}` such as a user's avatar. Square, round corners or a circle; *Fill* cuts off what doesn't fit, *Whole picture* shows all of it. |
| **Text** | In Regular, Bold or Monospace; left, centred or right in its width. Long texts wrap; *Shrink to fit* makes one line smaller until it fits (good for names). |
| **Bar** | A progress bar: *Value* out of *Out of*, such as `${xp}` out of `${needed}`. |

Click a layer in the picture (or the list) to choose it, drag it to move it, drag its corner to make it bigger or smaller (hold Shift to keep its shape). The arrow keys move it by a pixel, with Shift by ten. On the right are its settings: position, size, opacity, colour, a **gradient** to a second colour, an **outline**, and the rest of what its kind has.

The preview uses the same fonts as the bot, so what you see is what the bot draws, with two differences: pictures only show where they go (the bot loads them when it runs), and `${…}` shows its **preview value**.

### `${…}` in a design

Texts, pictures, bar values and colours can hold `${…}`: `${user.username}`, `${level}`, `${role.hexColor}`. As in other texts, a name that no earlier block gives gets an input on the block to connect.

Under the picture, **Preview values** has a box for each `${…}`: type what to show in the preview (`Alex` for `${user.username}`). They're only for the preview.

A user's avatar: `${user.displayAvatarURL({ extension: 'png', size: 256 })}`.

## Sending the picture

- Connect **File** to Send Message's **Files**.
- To show it inside an embed, put the block's **URL** (`attachment://canvas.png`) into the embed's image, and send the file with the message too.

**File name** changes `canvas.png`.

A picture that can't be loaded (a wrong address, say) is left out, with a warning in the Console; the rest is drawn.

## Under the hood

The bot draws with [@napi-rs/canvas](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@napi-rs/canvas), installed with the bot's other packages. The fonts (Ubuntu, Ubuntu Bold, Hack and Noto Emoji) come with the block, so exported bots draw the same on any server.

Fluxer bots send the picture the same way: Send Message's **Files**.


---

<!-- docs/explanations/alerts.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/alerts -->

# New-post alerts

::: info In short
**On New Post** runs once for each new video, post or release of a source you choose, and when a Twitch or Kick channel goes live. Connect it to Send Message to announce it.
:::

## Sources

| Source | What to write in *Channel* | Needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **YouTube channel** | `@handle`, the channel's link, or its id (`UC…`) | nothing. *Skip Shorts* leaves Shorts out. |
| **Twitch** (goes live) | the channel name, or its link | a client id and secret: Bot › Settings › New-post alerts |
| **Kick** (goes live) | the channel name, or its link | a client id and secret: Bot › Settings › New-post alerts |
| **Reddit** | the subreddit: `r/name` or `name` | nothing |
| **Bluesky** | the handle: `name.bsky.social` | nothing |
| **Mastodon** | `@name@server`, or the profile's link | nothing |
| **GitHub releases** | the repository: `owner/name` | nothing |
| **Steam news** | the game's app id (the number in its store link), or the link | nothing |
| **RSS or Atom feed** | the feed's address, under *Feed address* | nothing. Most blogs, news sites and podcasts have one. |

### Twitch and Kick keys

Both want an application of your own, which takes a minute and costs nothing:

- **Twitch:** at [dev.twitch.tv](https://dev.twitch.tv/console/apps) › Your Console › Applications › Register, with any name, the category *Chat Bot* and `http://localhost` as OAuth Redirect URL. Copy the **Client ID**, press **New Secret** and copy that too.
- **Kick:** at kick.com › Settings › Developer › Create app, with `http://localhost` as Redirect URL. Copy the **Client ID** and **Client Secret**.

Paste them into **Bot › Settings › New-post alerts**. The secrets are kept in the system's password store.

## What comes out

**Title**, **URL**, **Text** (without formatting, shortened), **Author**, **Image** (a thumbnail, when there is one) and **Date**. **Post** has all of it, with what the source has besides: `post.game` and `post.viewers` for streams, `post.nsfw` for Reddit, `post.short` for YouTube.

Announcing a new video in an embed: On New Post › Build Embed (title `${title}`, link `${url}`, image `${image}`) › Send Message to your channel.

## How it checks

- It looks every **Check every** minutes (5 by default; at least 1).
- **The first time**, posts that are already there only count as seen, so a new bot doesn't announce a channel's last 15 videos. Turn on *Announce what's there at first* to announce the newest few.
- **Nothing twice:** what it has seen is kept with the stored data, so a restart doesn't announce old posts again. More than 5 new posts at once (a feed that was off for a while): the 5 newest are announced.
- **Only if it contains** announces only posts whose title or text has a word or phrase.
- When a source can't be reached, the Console says so once and it keeps trying; it says when it works again.

Two On New Post blocks for the same channel each announce on their own (to two servers, say).


---

<!-- docs/explanations/server-tools.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/server-tools -->

# Server tools

::: info In short
The blocks in **Server Tools** look after servers: run commands over SSH, see CPU, memory and disk, restart Docker containers, send console commands to game servers (RCON), check a Minecraft server or any port. SSH, RCON and Docker only run once you allow them in **Bot › Settings › Server tools**.
:::

## Blocks

| Block | What it does | Needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SSH Command** | Runs a command on your server and gives what it printed, errors and exit code. | SSH in Bot › Settings, allowed |
| **Server Usage** | CPU %, memory, disk and uptime of the computer the bot runs on, or of an SSH server (Linux). | over SSH: allowed |
| **Docker** | Lists containers, starts, stops or restarts one, reads its latest log lines. | allowed; Docker on this computer, or `tcp://host:2375` |
| **RCON Command** | Sends a console command to a game server (Minecraft, Rust, ARK, CS2 …) and gives its answer. | RCON in Bot › Settings, allowed |
| **Minecraft Server** | Whether a Java or Bedrock server is up, players (and some names), version, message of the day, icon. | nothing |
| **Port Check** | Whether a server answers on a port, and how fast. | nothing |

Minecraft Server and Port Check say *offline* as an answer (with why), so a status message goes on instead of stopping.

## Safety

These blocks act on your servers, so:

- **They're off until you allow them**: Bot › Settings › Server tools › *Allow SSH, RCON and Docker*. Only turn it on for a bot whose commands you wrote yourself.
- **`${…}` in SSH Command is quoted for the shell.** `whitelist add ${name}` stays one command even if someone's name is `x; rm -rf ~`: the shell gets `'x; rm -rf ~'` as one word. Write `${…}` where a value goes, never around a whole command.
- **Use a user just for the bot** on the server, with only the rights it needs (no root), and a key rather than a password.
- **The server's key is remembered** the first time the bot connects. If it ever changes (another machine at that address), SSH Command refuses. After replacing the server on purpose, delete the stored value `hostkey:…` in the namespace `xc.server` (Stored Data view).
- Passwords, keys and the RCON password are kept in the system's password store, like the bot token.

## Servers given on the block

SSH Command, Server Usage, RCON Command and Docker can also connect to a server the block is **given**, instead of the one in Bot › Settings: set **Server** (Server Usage: *Where*) to *Given here*. Host, port and user are fields you can type or connect; the **password** and the **private key** can only be connected, from a slash command's option or a form, say. Typed into a block they'd be saved in the project file.

This needs its own switch, Bot › Settings › Server tools › *Allow servers given on blocks*, as well as *Allow SSH, RCON and Docker*. Anyone who can use such a command can make the bot connect where they say (to machines on your own network, too), so only turn it on for commands you trust them with: one only you or your staff can use.

- The password of Bot › Settings only ever goes to the server of Bot › Settings, never to one given on a block.
- SSH remembers each given server's key too, by host and port.
- A password typed into a normal message stays in the chat. Ask for it in a slash command's option or a form: only the bot sees those.

## Setting up

- **SSH:** host, port, user, and a password or a private key (the whole key text). Test with `SSH Command` running `whoami`.
- **RCON:** for Minecraft, in `server.properties`: `enable-rcon=true`, `rcon.port=25575`, `rcon.password=…`. Then host, port and password in Bot › Settings. Other servers: *Given here* (above).
- **Docker:** nothing when the bot runs on the same computer; the bot's user needs to be in the `docker` group. For Docker elsewhere: `tcp://host:2375` (only on a private network: Docker's API has no password).


---

<!-- docs/explanations/captcha.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/captcha -->

# Captcha

::: info In short
**Captcha** checks that someone is a person before they get in. It ends on **Passed**, **Failed** or **Timed Out**; connect Passed to Add Role, say.
:::

## Discord

A typical verification: a message with a **Verify** button in a `#verify` channel, an **On Button** for it, then **Captcha** with the button's **interaction**. The challenge appears in a message only that person sees.

| Mode | They… |
| --- | --- |
| **Type the code from a picture** | press *Answer* and type the code shown in a picture (letters that can't be mixed up; upper or lower case doesn't matter) |
| **Solve a sum** | press *Answer* and type the result, such as 7 × 6 |
| **Click the named emoji** | click the one of five emoji the message names (*Click the pizza*) |
| **Just click a button** | click *I'm a person*: the easiest, it stops only simple bots |

- **Tries** (3) and **Time** (3 minutes, in all). After a wrong answer they get a new challenge.
- **Where**: to the interaction (from a button or a slash command; only they see it), or as a **direct message** (from On Member Join, say; people can turn DMs off, so a button is more reliable).
- **Code length** for the picture: 4 to 8.

Then, for example: Passed › Add Role *Verified*; Failed › Moderate *kick*; Timed Out › Moderate *kick*, or nothing.

## Fluxer

Fluxer has no buttons yet, so its Captcha asks in a **channel**, mentioning the person, and waits for their answer there: the code from a picture, or a sum. *Clean up* (on) deletes the questions and answers afterwards.

## The picture

The bot draws it with the same package as [Build Canvas](./canvas) and brings its own font, so it works on any server.


---

<!-- docs/explanations/transcripts.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/transcripts -->

# Transcripts

::: info In short
**Create Transcript** saves a channel's messages as one HTML file that looks like Discord: for a ticket before it's closed, or a channel you archive. Send it with Send Message's **Files**, or keep it with **Write File**.
:::

## Using it

A ticket's *Close* button, for example: On Button › **Create Transcript** (the ticket's channel) › Send Message to a `#ticket-logs` channel with the transcript in **Files** › Delete Channel.

| Setting | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **At most** | The latest messages to keep (1000). 0 keeps all; in a long channel that takes a while. |
| **File name** | `transcript-${channel.name}.html` by default. |
| **Keep pictures** | Puts pictures into the file, so they still show when Discord's links expire. The file gets much bigger. |
| **Bots' messages too** | Off leaves out what bots wrote, such as the ticket's own buttons. |

It gives the **file**, how many messages it holds (**count**) and its **size**.

The file shows messages as Discord does: names and avatars, replies, embeds, Components V2 layouts, attachments, polls, threads. It opens in any browser.

## Safety

The bot needs **Read Message History** in the channel, and the *Message Content* intent (Bot › Settings › Privileged intents).

The transcript is drawn completely on the bot, so the file loads no scripts from the web, and what people wrote (names, messages) can't put code into it.

It uses [better-discord-transcripts](https://www.npmjs.com/package/better-discord-transcripts) 2.0.0, a version we read through before using it (no install scripts, nothing sent anywhere). It's installed with the bot the first time the block runs (with its helpers, about 80 MB).


---

<!-- docs/explanations/errors.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/errors -->

# Try Zones and errors

Things go wrong in bots: Discord says no, a member left a moment ago, a website is down. XC™ Circuit makes failures visible and gives you a way to deal with them.

## What happens when a block fails

When a block throws an error, its run stops there. The block turns red on the canvas, the Console says which block failed and why, and the other runs of the bot carry on. A failed run doesn't stop the bot.

If you have an **On Error** event, it runs when a block outside any Try Zone fails, with the message, the block's name and details: use it to log errors to a channel, for example.

## Try Zones

A Try Zone is a frame around some blocks that catches what goes wrong inside it. Select a block and choose **Try Zone** above it; drop more blocks in or out.

A zone has its own outputs:

- **Done**: the flow continues here when everything inside finished.
- **Error**: the flow continues here when something inside failed, with the error's **message** (and details) as outputs.

And two settings (the gear on the zone's title):

- **Retries**: try the blocks inside again this many times before giving up. Good for things that fail now and then, such as web requests.
- **Timeout**: give up when the blocks inside take longer than this.

If nothing is connected to **Error**, the zone logs a warning and the run ends there quietly: it doesn't count as a failure, and On Error doesn't run.

## Problems before running

The Problems panel lists what the editor can see before the bot runs, such as required fields that are empty or blocks from plugins that aren't installed. Click an entry to go to the block. Plugins can add their own [checks](/api/editor#xc-check).

## In your own blocks

A block fails by throwing: `throw new Error("No channel with that id")`. Write messages for the person building the bot: say what's wrong and, if you can, what to do about it.


---

<!-- docs/explanations/plugins.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/plugins -->

# Plugins

Almost everything in XC™ Circuit comes from plugins: the blocks, the Discord and Fluxer build modes, their pin types, the themes, the translations, the starters. The editor itself only knows how to load plugins, draw graphs and run bots. Even the bundled blocks are ordinary plugin files you can read in `plugins/`.

## What a plugin is

A folder with a [`plugin.toml`](/api/plugin-toml) that says what it contributes:

| Part | What it adds | Runs in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Blocks](/api/blocks) | blocks for the picker | the bot (and `define()` in the editor) |
| [Build modes](/api/build-modes) | a kind of bot: blocks, categories, settings, npm packages | — |
| [Runtime libraries](/api/runtime-libs) | shared code for a mode's blocks, such as the Discord client | the bot |
| [Pin types](/api/pin-types) | value types with colours and conversions | the bot (checks) and the editor |
| [Themes](/api/themes), [translations](/api/locales), [templates](/api/templates) | looks, languages, starters | the editor |
| [Editor script](/api/editor) | panels, commands, checks | the editor, sandboxed |

## Where plugins come from

XC Circuit loads plugins from:

- Folders listed in the `XC_CIRCUIT_PLUGINS` environment variable (handy while developing plugins).
- The **app's own** `plugins/` folder (Circuit Core, Discord Bot, Fluxer Bot).
- **Your plugins folder**: `%APPDATA%\XC Circuit\plugins` on Windows, `~/.local/share/xc-circuit/plugins` on Linux. Plugins › Open folder opens it.
- The open **project's** `plugins/` folder: plugins that belong to one bot and travel with it. XC Circuit asks before it loads them, once for each project folder and plugin: **Load this project's plugins?** lists them. Say yes for a project of your own or from someone you trust. With **Not now** the project opens without them (their blocks show as not installed), and Plugins › *Load This Project's Plugins…* asks again. A project's plugin can't take the place of one that comes with XC Circuit.

**Installing a plugin someone shared:** Plugins › *Install from Zip…* (or drop the `.zip` on the window). It goes into your plugins folder and loads right away. A zip holds the plugin folder: `plugin.toml` at its top, or in one folder at its top, as GitHub's *Download ZIP* makes them.

Plugin files are watched: saving a block, a theme or an editor script reloads it right away.

## Turning plugins off and removing them

The **Plugins view** in the side bar (the plug icon) lists every plugin. A plugin you installed has a switch, which turns it off (it stays listed, to turn on again), and a trash can, which removes it after you confirm. The plugins that come with the app say *Built in* and can't be turned off or removed. To make, test and share plugins, see the [Plugin guide](/plugins/).

## Block updates

The bundled blocks (Circuit Core, Discord Bot, Fluxer Bot) can get new versions without a new app version. When XC Circuit checks for updates (at start, unless turned off in Settings, and from Help › Check for Updates), it also asks the repository for newer versions of these plugins. If there are some, it lists them; **Update** downloads them, checks them and loads them right away. Projects keep working: blocks that changed are upgraded when a project opens, as after an app update.

**Help › Check for Updates** opens the **Updates** window. It shows whether a newer app is out, and for each bundled plugin the version you have and what's published: up to date, newer (**Update blocks** gets it), or needing a newer app. If GitHub couldn't be asked, it says why. **Download blocks again** downloads the published blocks again even when you have them, and replaces the downloaded copies: for when blocks seem out of date or broken.

Updates go into `plugin-updates` next to your plugins folder. **Help › Undo Block Updates** deletes them, and the blocks the app came with are back. When a later app version brings the same or newer blocks, those are used again by themselves: of two copies of a plugin, the higher version loads. An update that needs a newer app (`engines.app` in its plugin.toml) isn't offered to older apps.

For the people who make XC Circuit: changing a bundled plugin means raising its `version`, or the Checks on pull requests fail. When the version changes on `main`, the Plugins workflow publishes it.

## Editor code

Plugins change the editor with **editor scripts (JavaScript)**. Each runs in its own sandbox with a time and memory limit, and can only reach the app through the [`xc` object](/api/editor): read and change the project, add panels and commands, log. No files, no network, no programs. Because of that, scripts start without asking, also in a project you downloaded.

XC Circuit used to load compiled Rust libraries (native plugins) too. It doesn't any more: they had full access to your computer and had to be built with exactly the app's own compiler and libraries.

## Bot code is different

Blocks and runtime libraries don't run in the editor; they run in your **bot**, a Node.js program with the same access as any other program. That's the point: a bot needs the network, files and npm packages. Only use block plugins from people you trust, as you would with any npm package.


---

<!-- docs/explanations/running.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/running -->

# Running and exporting

## What Run does

Your bot is a Node.js program. When you press **Run** (F5), XC Circuit:

1. Makes sure **Node.js 22 or newer** is there (the first start page sets it up).
2. Installs the npm packages the build mode and its blocks need (discord.js, @fluxerjs/core, and any a block lists in `requires.dependencies`), once, into a shared packages folder. Packages your other bots installed there stay, so going from one bot to another doesn't install them again.
3. Bundles the runtime, your project and the blocks it uses into a run folder in the project's `.circuit/` folder.
4. Starts Node.js with the bot token from the credential store, and stays connected to it.

While the bot runs, the editor shows what it does: blocks glow when they run, failures turn them red, logs go to the Console, and the Stored Data view shows the bot's data. **Save** (Ctrl+S) restarts a running bot with your changes. **Stop** (Shift+F5) ends it.

The bot runs as its own process: if a block crashes Node.js, the editor is unaffected, and the editor can't freeze the bot.

## Answering in time

Discord waits 3 seconds for an answer to a slash command, button, select menu or form, and then shows *This interaction failed*.
