When the blocks after one take longer (creating a channel, a transcript, a web request), the bot answers for them after 2.5 seconds: a button or menu quietly (its message stays as it is, and Send Message's reply comes as a new message), a command or form with *thinking…*, which Send Message's reply then fills in (a private reply comes privately, and *thinking…* goes away). So **Defer** is only needed to show *thinking…* at once. A form (Show Modal) can't come after that: put it before slow blocks.

**Defer, then delete** answers with *thinking…* and takes it away again (after **Delete after** seconds; 0 as soon as it shows): the command or button counts as answered, and nothing stays. A reply after it comes as a new message. Send Message's **Delete after** also deletes replies, private ones too, through the interaction; Discord allows that for 15 minutes, later only messages the bot can see in their channel.

## What Export does

**Bot › Export…** writes a folder that runs on its own, without XC Circuit:

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `index.js` | the runtime, your project and its blocks in one file |
| `package.json` | the npm packages the bot needs |
| `.env` | the bot token and other secrets, if you chose to include them; otherwise empty lines to fill in |
| `.gitignore` | keeps `.env`, `node_modules/` and `data/` out of Git |
| `README.txt` | how to start it |

To start an exported bot anywhere Node.js runs (your PC, a server, a hosting service):

```bash
npm install
node index.js
```

The token is read from `.env` (`DISCORD_TOKEN=…` for Discord bots, `FLUXER_BOT_TOKEN=…` for Fluxer bots). Stored data goes into `data/`. Exporting again into the same folder keeps what you filled into `.env`.

An exported bot keeps itself running: `node index.js` watches the bot, starts it again a few seconds after a crash (waiting longer when it keeps crashing right away) and at once when a Restart block asks for it. A bot that can't start, because its token is missing or wrong, stays stopped. If something else already restarts your bot (pm2, systemd, Docker, a hosting panel), start it with `node index.js --no-restart` or set `XC_NO_RESTART=1`.

To put it on a server and keep it up to date there without copying files by hand, see [Putting your bot on a server](./hosting).

Exported bots are yours: you may run, share and sell them. See the [licence](https://github.com/XCraftTM/XC-Circuit/blob/main/LICENSE).


---

<!-- docs/explanations/hosting.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/hosting -->

# Putting your bot on a server

A bot only answers while it runs. Running it from the editor is fine while you build it; to keep it online, it runs on a server: a VPS, a computer at home, or a hosting service with a game panel. XC Circuit calls that place the bot's **remote**. **Bot › Remote…** puts it there for you, and can do that again after every save.

## How it gets there

Pick one in **Bot › Remote…**:

| | What you fill in | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SFTP** | the server's address, port (usually 22; game panels often use 2022), user name, and a password or a key file | a VPS or any server you can log in to with SSH, and most game panels |
| **Calagopus panel** | the panel's address; then **Sign in with the panel** and choose the server | servers on a [Calagopus](https://calagopus.com) panel: uploading, Start, Restart, Stop and the live console |

**Folder on the server** says where the bot's files go (it's made when missing). Left empty, they go where you start after logging in, or, on a Calagopus server, into the server's own folder.

Passwords and API keys are kept in your system's credential store, like the bot token (see [Tokens and safety](./safety)). The other settings are kept on your computer, in the project's `.circuit/local.json`: they are yours, not the bot's, so they aren't shared when you share the project or put it into Git. On another computer you fill them in once.

Your password, API key and the bot token only go to the server you last **saved** in Bot › Remote… on this computer: when that file names another one (another address, user, folder, the token turned on), because something else changed it or the project came with it, nothing is sent, the Console says so, and Bot › Remote… shows a note. Look the settings over and press **Save** to use them. Plugins' scripts and AI agents can't change the server.

## What is uploaded

The same files as [Export](./running#what-export-does): `index.js`, `package.json`, `.gitignore`, `README.txt`, and `.env` with the bot token and secrets while **Send the bot token** is on. Turn that off to fill in `.env` on the server yourself.

Only files that changed since the last upload to the same place are sent; uploading an unchanged bot sends nothing. Nothing else on the server is touched: its `data/` folder (what the bot saved) and `node_modules/` stay as they are.

The server needs Node.js 22 or newer. It runs `npm install` itself: the Node.js servers of game panels do that when they start; on your own server, run `npm install` once, then start it with `node index.js` (or a service manager such as pm2 or systemd).

## Uploading

- **Save and upload** in Bot › Remote…, **Bot › Upload to the remote**, or the item at the bottom right of the window (it also shows how the last upload went: click it for the details).
- With **Upload after every save** on, Ctrl+S also puts the new version on the server.
- On a Calagopus server, **Restart the server after uploading** (on at first) restarts it, so the new version runs right away. On other servers, restart the bot yourself.

**Test connection** logs in and out again, to check the settings without uploading.

## SFTP: the server's key

The first time XC Circuit connects to an SFTP server, it keeps the server's key (its fingerprint shows in the upload's messages). Later connections check that the server still shows the same key. If it shows another one, the upload stops: that can mean the address now leads to another computer. If your server really got a new key (it was reinstalled), remove its line from `known_hosts.json` in XC Circuit's data folder and upload again.

## Calagopus

**Sign in with the panel** opens the panel's page for making an API key in your browser, with the permissions XC Circuit needs: reading your servers, their console, Start, Stop and Restart, and writing files. Approve it there, and the panel hands the key back to XC Circuit (on a one-time address on your computer). The key is named after the bot, such as *XC Circuit · Test Bot #a1b2* (the tag keeps it apart from earlier keys, as a panel takes each name once). You can also make a key yourself in the panel (Account › API Keys) and paste it: it needs the servers.read permission, and the servers are listed as soon as it's in. Then choose the server in the list.

**Bot › Remote console** shows the chosen server: its state, CPU and memory, **Start**, **Restart**, **Stop** and **Kill** (ends it at once, without letting it save), and its live console, in the colours the server prints (as in the panel). Like the Console, it can be a tab anywhere or an icon in the activity bar, shown in the side bar (drag its tab there). Left open when you close XC Circuit, the console tab comes back, connected, the next time it starts with that project.

### Running the bot on the server

With a Calagopus server chosen and signed in, a **Local | Remote** switch shows beside **Run** at the top right. Pick **Remote**, and Run, Restart and Stop (the buttons, F5 and Shift+F5, the Bot menu and the status bar) act on the server instead of this computer:

- **Run** uploads what changed, then starts the server, so it runs the version you see. When it runs already, the button says **Restart**: it uploads, then restarts it.
- **Stop** stops the server.
- The status bar shows the server's state (*Remote running*, *starting*, *stopping*, *stopped*), read every few seconds; hover it for the server's name, CPU and memory.

Picking Remote stops the bot running here, so the two don't both answer. The switch is kept per project; **Local** puts Run back on this computer (the server keeps running).


---

<!-- docs/explanations/git.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/git -->

# Keeping a project in Git

A project is a folder of small text files, so it fits well in a Git repository: on GitHub, GitLab, Gitea or any other place that speaks Git over HTTPS. That gives you the bot on several computers, a history of every version, and a way to work on it with others. **File › Git…** does it from inside XC Circuit; you don't need Git installed.

## Setting it up

**File › Git…** leads you through it the first time: what is stored and what never is, an account (with a button to make one on GitHub), a repository (with a button to make one), and then the form:

1. Paste the repository's **HTTPS address** (the page shows it under *Code* or *Clone*; it starts with `https://`, not `git@`).
2. Sign in:
   - **GitHub:** press **Sign in with GitHub**. A page opens in your browser; type in the code XC Circuit shows and approve. No password goes through the app.
   - **Anywhere else, or if you prefer:** make an **access token** in your account's settings there, allowed to read and write repositories (GitHub: *Developer settings › Personal access tokens*; GitLab: *Access tokens* with `write_repository`; Gitea: *Applications*), and paste it.
3. Press **Connect**.

The sign-in is kept in your system's credential store, one per place (`github.com`, your own Gitea …), for all your projects there. It is never written into the project.

## A project without a folder of its own

A project kept in a Git repository doesn't need a folder you look after. **File › New Project…** offers **In a Git repository** beside **Only on this computer**, and **Get from Git…** offers **Kept by XC Circuit**: the project then lives in the app's own folder (on Windows under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\XC Circuit\remotes`), as a complete copy you can work on without a network, and stays in your recent projects. **Show the folder** in File › Git… opens it. Choose a folder of your own instead when the project has files you reach by their path, such as pictures.

**Disconnect…** in File › Git… forgets the repository: the project and its history stay on the computer, and what is stored there stays there. **Disconnect and keep as a folder…** also moves a project out of the app's folder into one you choose. **Remove from this computer…** deletes a copy the app keeps, after asking once more: what is in the repository stays, but changes not stored yet and the bot's own data on that computer are gone for good.

## Store and Fetch

Once connected, XC Circuit keeps the two in step **by itself**: every save is stored and sent, what others stored comes in with it, and when the project opens the newest version is fetched first. Without a network you just keep working; the next save catches up. **Keep in step by itself** in File › Git… turns that off for this computer; then it happens when you press:

- **Store** saves the project, records what changed since the last time (with the few words you give it) and sends it to the repository.
- **Fetch** gets what is stored there and puts it together with what you have here. Your own changes are recorded first, so nothing of yours is lost.

When newer changes are stored there, Store says so: press **Fetch** first, then **Store** again.

## Earlier versions

Every Store is a version. **Earlier versions** in File › Git… lists the newest ones with their words, who stored them and when. **Go back to this** makes the project what it was then, as a new version on top: nothing in between is lost, and you can go back to where you were the same way.

## Before something secret is stored

When a block holds something that looks like a secret (a webhook address, a bot token, an access key), Store stops and shows where. Whoever can read the repository could read it. Keep such things in **Bot › Settings** instead; or press **Store anyway** if it is meant to be there.

## On another computer

**File › Get from Git…** (also on the start page) brings a stored project onto a computer: paste the repository's address, choose where its folder goes, sign in if the repository is private, and press **Get the project**. It opens right away. Then fill in the bot token once in **Bot › Settings**; it was never stored.

## When both changed the same thing

The project's files are put together by what they hold, not line by line: every setting of a block on its own, wires one by one. So two people can work in the same workspace: one changes a block's message while the other adds blocks and wires, and both arrive. Where a block sits never stands in the way; if both moved it, yours stays.

Blocks are told apart by a fixed id, not by their number. When two people both add a "block 7", those are two blocks: the one already stored keeps the number, the other gets the next free one, and its wires and every `${#7.…}` that reads it follow.

Only where both changed the **same setting** in different ways (or one deleted a block the other changed) XC Circuit **changes nothing** and asks, part by part, saying what it is about: *The note “Ideas” in Main: changed here, deleted in the stored version*, or *Block #4 (core.log) in Main: changed here and in the stored version, in different ways*. Choose for each whose version stays, **Mine** or **The stored one**; for a block there is also **Both**, which keeps yours and puts the other one beside it as a block of its own. Then press **Put together**. What you didn't pick stays in the repository's history.

The two versions are put together in memory first; the project's folder only changes once the result is whole.

## What is stored, and what never is

Stored: `circuit.project.json`, `workspaces/`, `commands/`, and whatever else you keep in the folder (the project's own plugins, pictures).

Never stored: the `.circuit/` folder. That is this computer's part: where the bot is uploaded to, database connections, private settings, the bot's stored data. And the bot token and passwords are not in the project's files at all; they stay in the credential store. On another computer you fill in the token once in **Bot › Settings**.

## Good to know

- A repository you set up yourself with Git works too: File › Git… uses it as it is, and adds `.circuit/` to its `.gitignore`.
- Files are stored byte for byte, whatever line-ending setting your own Git has, so a project is the same on Windows and Linux.
- When a project opens, XC Circuit looks whether newer versions are stored there (nothing is changed), so the status bar can say **Git: 2 to fetch**.
- The status bar shows how the project stands: **Git: stored**, or how many changes wait to be stored or fetched. Click it to open File › Git…. Store, Fetch and the dialog can each get a shortcut in Settings › Shortcuts.


---

<!-- docs/explanations/host.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/host -->

# The Host: a place of your own

The **XC Circuit Host** is a small server you run yourself, in a Docker container. It is for people who want their projects on a machine of their own instead of GitHub, and it is what live sessions go through.

::: warning Work in progress
The container is here and tested, and from XC Circuit you can pair with it, keep projects on it and carry a project's secrets between your devices. [Live sessions](live.md) can meet at your host instead of the public relay. Running the bot on the host is still being built.
:::

## What it does

| | What it keeps |
| --- | --- |
| **Projects** | Your projects with every version, as Git repositories: XC Circuit keeps in step with it the same way as with GitHub. |
| **Vault** | Your bots' secrets (token, passwords), **encrypted by your devices**. The host can't read them, and neither can someone who gets hold of its data. |
| **Relay** | Nothing: it passes the messages of a live session from one app to the others. |

It has two modes, set with `XC_HOST_MODE`:

- **`full`** (the default): all three. It needs a data folder (a volume); without one it doesn't start, and says so, instead of writing into the container where an update would wipe it.
- **`relay`**: only the relay. Nothing is kept, no volume is needed. This is what a public relay runs.

## Setting it up

You need a server with Docker and a reverse proxy that adds HTTPS, such as Nginx Proxy Manager.

1. Get [`host/docker-compose.yml`](https://github.com/XCraftTM/XC-Circuit/blob/main/host/docker-compose.yml) and start it. It uses the published image, `ghcr.io/xcrafttm/xc-circuit-host` (for x64 and ARM); in Portainer, a stack with the same file does it:

   ```bash
   docker compose -f host/docker-compose.yml up -d
   ```

   The compose file puts the host on your proxy's Docker network (change the network's name to yours) and publishes **no port**: it is only reachable through the proxy.

2. In the proxy, add a host for your domain (say `circuit.example.com`) that forwards to `http://xc-circuit-host:7421`, with **Websockets Support** on, a certificate, and **Force SSL**.

3. Open `https://circuit.example.com/status`. It answers with its mode and protocol version:

   ```json
   { "name": "xc-circuit-host", "version": "0.3.0", "protocol": 1, "mode": "full", "can": ["relay", "projects", "vault"] }
   ```

4. Pair your first device. There is no password to start with: the host prints a code in its log, good for ten minutes (restart it for a new one):

   ```bash
   docker compose -f host/docker-compose.yml logs xc-circuit-host
   ```

   In XC Circuit, open **File › Host…**, fill in the host's address and that code, and press **Pair**.

## Your devices

The first device makes the **key your secrets are sealed with**, and shows it once as a **recovery code**: write it down. Your devices pass the key on to each other; if all of them are ever gone, the recovery code is the only way to read the secrets on the host again (tick *I have a recovery code* when pairing the next first device).

Every further device comes in through one that is paired already:

1. On the paired device: **File › Host… › Add a device**. It shows a code of 16 letters and digits. Leave that window open.
2. On the new device: **File › Host…**, the host's address and that code, **Pair**.

Half of the code goes to the host, which lets the device in. The other half only travels from one screen to the other keyboard: the two devices use it to pass the key on, so the host can't get at it even if it tried.

**Unpair this computer…** takes it off the host's list and deletes its token and its key here.

## A project on the host

With a project open, File › Host… has three buttons:

- **Keep this project on the host** stores it there and keeps it in step from then on: every save goes to the host, and what another of your devices stores comes in by itself, as the host tells every connected device at once that something changed. The dialog then says that the project is kept there and how it stands. (It is the same as [with GitHub](git.md) underneath; File › Git… shows the details and the earlier versions.)
- **Send its secrets** seals the bot token and the project's other secrets on this computer and puts them in the host's vault.
- **Get its secrets** fetches them on another device and saves them in that computer's credential store. No more typing the token in on every device.

The passwords for uploading the bot from one computer (Bot › Remote…) don't travel: they belong to that computer.

On another device, get the project with **File › Get from Git…** and the address `https://circuit.example.com/git/my-bot.git`; once paired, that device is signed in there already.

## Settings

| Variable | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `XC_HOST_MODE` | `full` | `full` or `relay`. |
| `XC_HOST_PORT` | `7421` | The port inside the container. Not a port of any common service, and never open to the internet: the proxy is. |
| `XC_HOST_DATA` | `/data` | Where full mode keeps everything: `host.sqlite` and `projects/`. |
| `XC_HOST_TRUSTED_PROXY` | (none) | Whose word to take for an app's address (`X-Forwarded-For`), to limit misuse per person: `private` for a proxy on a private network, or the proxy's addresses, separated by commas. |

## Good to know

- **Backups are yours to make.** Everything is in the data volume: copy it while the container is stopped, or with a snapshot.
- **The proxy sees the traffic**, as it adds the HTTPS. That is fine: secrets are encrypted by your devices before they are sent, and live sessions are encrypted between the apps.
- **Limits** keep one person from filling it up: 16 guests in a session, 4 sessions and 32 connections per address, 256 KB per message, 64 KB of secrets per project. A code for pairing runs out after 10 minutes; a key nobody fetched, after 30 days.
- The host and the app are updated on their own, so they tell each other their **protocol version** first.
- A sign of life goes both ways every 30 seconds, as proxies cut connections that say nothing (Nginx after 60 seconds).

## For developers: the messages

Everything but Git goes over one WebSocket at `/ws`, as JSON with a `t`:

| From the app | Answer | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `open` | `opened { room }` | Starts a live session. Its host owns it: when they leave, it ends (`closed`). |
| `join { room }` | `joined { you }` | The session's host gets `peer { id, on }`. |
| `to { data, id? }` | | A guest's goes to the host; the host's to one guest (`id`) or all. Arrives as `from { id, data }`. `data` is the apps' own, encrypted by them. |
| `kick { id }`, `leave`, `ping` | `pong` | |
| `pair { code, name, key }` | `paired { device, token }` | Full mode. `key` is the device's public key, for the others to wrap the vault's key for it. |
| `hello { token }` | `welcome { device, name }` | Says who this is. Needed for all below. |
| `invite` | `invited { code, minutes }` | A code for one more device. |
| `devices`, `device.remove { id }` | `devices { devices, you }` | |
| `vault.get { project }` | `vault { blob, rev }` | |
| `vault.put { project, blob, rev }` | `vault.kept { rev }` | `rev` is the one last seen: a newer one there refuses it. |
| `key.put { for, blob }`, `key.get` | `keys { keys }` | A key wrapped for another device, kept until it fetches it. |
| | `project.changed { project, by }` | Sent to every connected device when something was stored in a project: time to fetch. |

What goes wrong comes back as `error { re, why }`. The source is one file, [`host/server.js`](https://github.com/XCraftTM/XC-Circuit/blob/main/host/server.js), with no dependencies beyond Node.js 24 and Git; `node host/test/host.js` runs its tests.


---

<!-- docs/explanations/live.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/live -->

# Live sessions: working together

In a live session several people work in one project at the same time. One of them **hosts**: the project is theirs, it is saved on their computer, and the bot runs there. The others are **guests**: they see every change as it happens, and may change what the host lets them.

::: warning New
Live sessions are new in 0.3.0. Stored Data and where the bot is uploaded to stay with the host; a guest doesn't see them.
:::

## Starting one

1. Open the project and **File › Live session…**
2. Give yourself a name, and press **Start a session for this project**.
3. **Copy** the invitation and send it to the people you want in. It starts with `xc-live:`. Whoever has it can join, so only give it to them.

The session meets at a **relay**: the public one (`https://xcrelay.xcrafttm.dev`), or [your own host](host.md) if you put its address there. The relay only passes messages on. It can't read them: everything is sealed with a key that is part of the invitation, and so only travels from you to your guests.

## Joining one

On the start page: **Join a live session…**, your name, paste the invitation, **Join** (File › Live session… has the same). The host's project opens. It is a copy for this session, kept in the app's own folder; it is saved at the host's, not at yours. When the session is over, the copy closes and you are back on the start page.

Host and guests need the **same version** of XC Circuit. If they differ, the guest isn't let in and is told who has to update.

### Plugins the host has and you don't

The plugins that come with XC Circuit are the same for everyone. Others the host uses (ones they installed, or the project's own) are passed on to you, into your copy of the project: they never replace a plugin of your own. They are someone else's code, so XC Circuit **asks before it loads them**, as with any project that brings plugins along. Say no and the session still works; blocks from those plugins then show as unknown. A plugin of more than 4 MB isn't passed on.

### When your connection drops

Your app tries to get back in by itself, for about two minutes. Back in, you are who you were, with what the host let you do; your copy catches up with what happened meanwhile, and what you changed while away is sent after all. If the host's own connection drops, the session is over.

## Seeing each other

Everyone has a colour. On the canvas you see the others' **pointers** with their names, gliding along as they move, in the workspace they are in, and a block someone has **selected** is framed in their colour with their name on it: so two people don't change the same block without noticing.

## What guests may do

A new guest only **watches**. The host ticks, per guest, what they may change, and can change that at any time:

| | Lets a guest |
| --- | --- |
| **The bot (start, stop)** | start and stop the bot, which runs at the host's; Run and Stop in the guest's window do it |
| **Slash commands** | make, change and delete commands |
| **Workspaces** | make, rename, move, turn on and off, and delete workspaces |
| **Blocks, everywhere** | change blocks, wires and notes in every workspace |
| **Blocks in:** (some workspaces) | the same, in the ticked workspaces only |
| **Servers, channels, roles** | pick from the bot's servers, channels and roles in a block's fields; without it a field only shows the id that is in it |
| **Values on wires** | see what went through the wires when the bot ran: real members' names and messages |

The host checks every change against this before taking it. A change a guest may not make is taken back at the guest's, with a word why. Bot settings, secrets, where the bot is uploaded to and plugins are the host's alone. **Send away** removes a guest.

## When several change the same thing

Changes are put together the way they are when [two stored versions meet](git.md): every setting of a block on its own, wires one by one. Two people can work in the same workspace, even on the same block.

- Where two change the **same setting** at the same moment, the **host's** stays (or, between guests, the one that reached the host first). Nobody is asked.
- Two blocks that got the same number are two blocks: the host's keeps the number, the other gets the next free one, with its wires and what reads it.
- Where a block sits is everyone's own business until they move it: a move travels like any other change.

**Undo** only takes back your own work. What the others did in between stays.

## The bot, and ending

The bot runs only at the host's: the token never leaves their computer. What it writes to the **Console** shows at every guest's too (secrets are hidden there as always), and File › Live session… says whether it runs. A guest's Run button shows how the bot stands at the host's (Run, Starting…, Restart, with Stop beside it). A guest the host ticked **The bot** for starts and stops it with their own Run and Stop; for the others, Run says that it is the host's to start.

Every guest sees **which blocks ran**, how long they took, and where one failed, lit up on the canvas as at the host's. The values on the wires are for guests with that tick only.

## What the bot's token is for

A guest has no token. Whatever needs it, the host's app reads and passes on, and only what it shows itself: how the bot looks (its name and picture, for the previews: every guest gets that, so previews look the same for all) and, for guests with the tick, the list of servers with their channels and roles. A guest can't ask Discord for anything else through the host, and nothing on this way changes anything at Discord.

**End the session** (the host) ends it for everyone; **Leave the session** (a guest) only for that guest. When the host's app closes or loses its connection, the session is over. A guest's copy stays open as it was, but it is only a copy: what counts is the host's project.


---

<!-- docs/explanations/ai-agents.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/ai-agents -->

# AI agents (MCP)

AI agents such as Claude can work on your bot in XC Circuit: look at your workspaces, add blocks and wire them up, fix problems, and start the bot to try it. They do it through XC Circuit's **MCP server** ([Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)), which comes with the app in the **AI agents (MCP)** plugin.

## Add it to your AI client

Open **Plugins › AI agents panel**. For each AI client found on your computer there's a button:

| Client | What **Add** does | Then |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Desktop | adds XC Circuit to `claude_desktop_config.json` | quit and reopen Claude Desktop |
| Claude Code | runs `claude mcp add --scope user xc-circuit …` | start a new Claude Code session |
| Cursor | adds it to `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | restart Cursor |
| VS Code | adds it to your user `mcp.json` | it shows under MCP servers in the Chat view |

For any other MCP client, **Copy settings** copies the entry to paste into its MCP settings:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "xc-circuit": { "command": "C:\\…\\XC Circuit\\xc-circuit.exe", "args": ["--mcp"] }
  }
}
```

The panel shows **Added, but for another copy of XC Circuit** when the entry points to a different `xc-circuit` (after moving the app, say): **Update** points it here. **Remove** takes it out again. Before changing a settings file for the first time, XC Circuit keeps a copy next to it (`….json.before-xc-circuit`).

## Use it

Keep XC Circuit open with your project, and ask the agent, for example: *"Add a /ping command that answers with the bot's ping"*. If XC Circuit isn't open, the agent sees one tool, `open_xc_circuit`, which opens it. When XC Circuit opens or closes later, the server tells the AI client that its tools changed, so the client picks up the full set (or loses it) by itself, without reconnecting.

What the agent can do:

| Tool | |
| --- | --- |
| `get_project` | the project, its workspaces, problems and slash commands |
| `get_workspace` · `get_block` | a workspace's blocks and wires · one block's values and pins |
| `find_block_types` · `get_block_type` | the installed blocks and their fields |
| `add_block` · `set_block_values` · `move_block` · `delete_blocks` | change blocks |
| `connect` · `disconnect` | wires, checked like ones you draw |
| `create_workspace` · `get_slash_commands` · `set_slash_commands` | workspaces and commands |
| `add_note` · `set_note` · `delete_note` | notes on the canvas, also framing blocks you name |
| `open_builder` | opens the Embed, Layout or Canvas Builder (or Slash Commands) on a block, to show you |
| `screenshot` | a picture of the canvas (a workspace fitted to view, or centred on a block, at a zoom it picks if it likes), so the agent sees what it built |
| `get_problems` · `get_console` | what's wrong, and what the bot logged |
| `list_block_types` · `get_block_source` · `list_plugins` | every block, a block's code (to see exactly what it does), the plugins |
| `get_app_settings` · `get_bot_settings` · `set_bot_settings` | XC Circuit's settings (to read), and Bot › Settings (to read and change; never the token) |
| `get_server` · `server_action` · `set_run_target` | the bot's server: its state, the last upload and its console; upload, start, restart, stop, kill; and whether Run acts here or there |
| `run_bot` · `stop_bot` · `save_project` · `show_in_editor` | run it (here or on the server), save it, show you a block |
| `run_script` | many of these at once: JavaScript that gets every tool as a function (`tools.add_block({ … })`), the [plugin API](/api/editor) as `xc`, and `print()` |

Embeds, layouts and canvases are what Build Embed, Build Layout and Build Canvas keep in a field: agents fill them with `set_block_values`, and `get_block_type` tells them the format. Embeds and layouts can also be given as Discord's own JSON, as in the builders' JSON tab.

`run_script` lets an agent build a whole flow in one step instead of a call per block. It runs in the same sandbox as plugins: no files, no network, at most 5 seconds.

Every tool the agent uses is written to the **Console** as an **MCP** line ("AI agent: add_block · workspace main, type "core.log""), with the reason when it failed and **Show block** when it's about one. The **MCP** chip above the Console shows only those. Every change shows in the editor right away and can be undone with **Ctrl+Z**, like your own.

**The token.** No tool gives an agent the bot's token or another secret, agents can't change where the bot is uploaded to, and when the bot prints a secret, the Console (which the agent can read) shows `[hidden secret]` instead. An agent does build and run your bot, though, and a running bot has its token, as it must: let agents you trust work on bots whose tokens matter.

## How it works

The AI client starts `xc-circuit --mcp`, which speaks MCP over its input and output. It passes the agent's requests to the running app through a connection on your computer only (`127.0.0.1`, with a secret written to XC Circuit's data folder, in a file only you can read). A program that connects without the secret is let go. The app answers them with the plugins' tools: plugins can add their own with [`xc.tool`](/api/editor#xc-tool).

## Turn it off

Under **Plugins**, switch **AI agents (MCP)** off: the server stops listening and agents see only `open_xc_circuit`. The trash can removes it; it comes with the app, so **Add back** at the end of the Plugins list brings it back.


---

<!-- docs/explanations/safety.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/safety -->

# Tokens and safety

## The bot token never goes into the project

A bot token is a password: whoever has it controls the bot. XC™ Circuit keeps tokens and other secrets (settings marked `secret` by a build mode, such as music service logins) in your operating system's credential store:

- **Windows**: Credential Manager
- **Linux**: the Secret Service (GNOME Keyring, KWallet)

The project folder never contains them, so you can put a project in Git, share it or send it to someone for help without leaking the token. In Bot › Settings the eye button shows what you're typing, and Copy copies the saved token without showing it.

While the bot runs from the editor, the Console hides its secrets: if the bot prints its token or a saved login (a Log block with `${process.env…}` would), `[hidden secret]` shows instead, also in a block's values on a wire and in errors. That keeps them out of screenshots and screen shares, and away from plugins' scripts and AI agents that read the Console. It doesn't make secrets unreachable for the bot's own code: blocks need the token, and code you run in your bot can use it.

An exported bot reads its token from `.env`. Export only includes the token there when you ask it to, and its `.gitignore` keeps `.env` out of Git.

The passwords and API keys for uploading the bot to its server (Bot › Remote…) are kept in the credential store too. An upload sends the token in `.env` only while **Send the bot token** is on; over FTP, keep **Encrypted (FTPS)** on, as plain FTP sends it unencrypted. They, and the token, only go to the server you saved in Bot › Remote… on this computer, not to one that came with a project's files. See [Putting your bot on a server](./hosting).

## What editor plugins can do

[Editor scripts](/api/editor) run in a sandbox (QuickJS) inside the editor:

- They reach the app **only** through the `xc` object: the open project, panels, commands, the Console, their own small storage.
- They have **no** access to files, the network, other programs or your secrets.
- Each call has a **time limit** (an endless loop is stopped) and each plugin a **memory limit**.

That's why installed plugins' scripts start without asking. A script of a plugin that doesn't come with XC Circuit can start the bot, or upload it, only when you click one of its buttons or pick one of its commands, not by itself.

## Plugins that come with a project

A project can bring plugins of its own, in its `plugins/` folder: handy for blocks made for one bot, but with a project from someone else that is their code. XC Circuit asks before it loads them (**Load this project's plugins?**), once for each project folder and plugin, and remembers the answer on your computer, not in the project. Until you say yes, nothing of those plugins is read or run. A project's plugin never replaces one that comes with XC Circuit, such as Discord Bot, which handles your token.

## What bot code can do

Blocks run in your bot, which is a normal Node.js program. A block can read files, use the network and start programs, because bots need to. Treat block plugins like npm packages: use ones from people you trust, and read the code of ones you don't know. Blocks are plain JavaScript files, so you can.


---

<!-- docs/explanations/editor-reference.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/explanations/editor-reference -->

<!-- Kept from the README: every feature of the editor, one row each. -->
# Everything the editor does

| Action | How |
| --- | --- |
| Add a block | Add block in the canvas toolbar (bottom left), right-click empty canvas, or press Space |
| Connect | Drag from a pin to another pin. Holding the wire at an edge of the canvas moves the canvas that way, for blocks out of view |
| Add a connected block | Drag a wire into empty space; the picker shows only compatible blocks |
| Move a block | Drag its title bar |
| Pan / zoom | Drag empty canvas or middle mouse / mouse wheel |
| Templates | File › New Project starts empty or from a working bot, grouped by kind. Discord: Welcome & auto role, Levels & XP, Role menu, Reminders, Moderation, Tickets (with a transcript), Verify with a captcha, New-post alerts, Minecraft server status (in `examples/templates/`). Fluxer: Basic commands, Reminders, Moderation, Verify with a captcha, New-post alerts, Minecraft server status. A plugin adds its own in a `templates` folder; `template.json` gives each its `category` and `icon` |
| JavaScript in texts | Any text field (Send Message, Log, Text, the Embed and Layout Builders …) can hold JavaScript in `${…}`, as in a JavaScript template string: `${user.username}`, `${xp * 2}`, `${member?.nickname ?? user.username}`, `${new Date().getFullYear()}`. `#4` is block #4's outputs: `${#4.message.url}`. Names come from the event, run variables, the block's fields and earlier outputs; a name nothing earlier gives gets an input below the text to connect a value to. A mistake in an expression stops the block with an error naming it. Texts from before, with `{name}`, are changed to `${name}` when a project opens |
| Values from earlier blocks | Type `${` in any text (on a block, in the Inspector or a builder), or right-click it, for the values the block can use. `${` lists the blocks before this one on its action path; pick one and the list slides to its values (`${#1.user}`, the User output of block #1), and › (or →) goes on to a value's members; ← goes back. Typing a name, or a `.` after a value, inside `${…}` lists what fits with its type, like a code editor: `${#1.user.username}`, `${#1.member.roles.highest.name}`, `${#1.user.displayAvatarURL()}`. Run variables are `${name}`. The Embed, Layout and Modal Builders list the values too, under the preview: click one to put it where the text cursor is. **Hide** puts the list away so the preview gets its room (**Show** brings it back); drag the line between the preview and the list to share the room differently |
| Members of Discord values | They come from discord.js itself: `plugins/xc.discord/types/discordjs.classes.json` is made from discord.js's type definitions by `node plugins/xc.discord/tools/discordjs-catalog.js` (run it again after updating discord.js). Only methods that read are listed |
| Message previews | The Embed and Layout Builders show the message as Discord will: with the bot's own name and picture (read from Discord with the saved bot token, when there is one) and each `${…}` as a chip, since its value is only known when the bot runs |
| One path per action | An action output leads to one block: connecting it to another block replaces the old wire. Paths can join, and branch only through blocks made for it (If, Switch, For Each). Older projects with split paths show them in Problems |
| Yes/no inputs | Switches like Private reply can be connected too: click their pin toggle in the Inspector |
| Long text | Text fields on blocks are boxes of a few lines; drag a box's corner down to make it taller or shorter and sideways to make the whole block wider or narrower (the block saves both in the project), double-click the corner to reset them |
| Emoji | Emoji show in colour, as in Discord, with the computer's own emoji font (Segoe UI Emoji on Windows, Noto Color Emoji on Linux); symbols the editor uses as marks (▶ ⚠ ✔ ™ arrows) stay plain. Without an emoji font they're black and white |
| Wider blocks | Blocks that show a message, embed or form (Build Layout, Build Embed, Show Modal …) get as wide as it is in Discord by themselves: a row of buttons fits on one line, and long text stops at Discord's widest and wraps. A block with a big text box gets wider when you drag that box's corner sideways |
| Colors | Click a color swatch for the picker: square and hue bar, hex and RGB, Discord colors and your recent ones. The `${}` button next to it takes a color from the bot instead, such as `${role.hexColor}` or `${color}`: hex, with or without `#` (FF5CA8 works too). Block color fields (Create Role's) can also be a pin to connect a value to; the Embed, Layout and Canvas Builders' colors take `${…}`, each name getting an input on the block |
| Field as pin | Click a field's faint pin, or "pin" in the Inspector |
| More options | Options used less often are folded below **More options** at the bottom of its fields (click it to open or fold them; each block remembers). Folded, an option in use (connected, a pin, or set to something) still shows. The Inspector lists them under More options |
| Accessibility | Settings › Window › Accessibility (on to start with) lets screen readers and the touch keyboard see what's in the window. If XC Circuit stops answering while a program that reads windows runs, try turning it off; freezes.log says whether it was on |
| Select several | Shift-drag a box on empty canvas, or Ctrl+click blocks; Ctrl+A selects all |
| Block actions | Select a block: Duplicate, Try Zone, Note and Delete are buttons above it (Delete key works too), in two rows when the block is narrow. The Inspector's Block source shows the block's source file in its folder |
| Remove a wire | Click it, then its Delete wire button (or press Delete); or drag it off its input and drop it on empty canvas |
| Zoom | The canvas toolbar: − / + , the percentage goes back to 100%, the corners button shows every block; or the mouse wheel |
| Undo / Redo | Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y (per workspace). Each workspace keeps 200 steps; Settings › Editor › Undo steps changes that (every step is a copy of the workspace, so fewer use less memory on big projects) |
| Copy / Paste / Duplicate | Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V (at the mouse) / Ctrl+D; works across workspaces and projects. A `${#7.…}` in a pasted text points at the pasted copy of block #7 when it was copied along; Problems lists texts that use a block number the workspace doesn't have |
| First start | The welcome page sets up Node.js (finds it, or installs it: winget or the official installer on Windows, a private copy on Linux), a theme and an accent; Help › Welcome and setup… opens it again |
| Workspaces in order | Drag a workspace above or below another (a line shows where), or onto a folder to move it there. Drag a folder onto the middle of another to put it in there (folders go in folders, as deep as you like), onto its top or bottom edge to put it above or below, or onto the project row to bring it back to the top. While dragging, a label at the pointer says what letting go does ("Into Events", "Below Startup, in Commands"; red where it can't go), the dragged row stays faded in its place, a folder held over for a moment opens, and the list scrolls near its top and bottom edges. A folder's menu has **New folder here**; deleting a folder moves what's in it up a level. The order is saved with the project |
| Side bar | Git, Host and Live session can be dragged there too, like the panels. The activity bar's icon picks what it shows (Workspaces, Stored Data, Plugins to start with); clicking the one shown folds it away. Two at once: drag an icon (or one of those tabs) onto the side bar's lower half, or right-click an icon › Show in the lower half; it shows under the first, and the line between them drags to share the height. Right-click a half's name to swap the halves, close one, or move it to the main area; clicking an icon that shows hides that half. The icons work like tabs: drag one to reorder them, or out onto the main area to make it a tab there. Drag a tab (Workspaces, Inspector, Console, Problems, the Server console, a plugin's panel) onto the activity bar to make it an icon. Right-click an icon › Move to the main area. View › Side bar and View › Panels tick what's open, as an icon or a tab: untick to take it away, tick to bring it back (Workspaces, Stored Data and Plugins into the activity bar, panels as a tab). Narrow, Settings and Bot settings show their pages as a dropdown |
| Tour | Help › Take the tour: build a tiny bot on a practice project. What to click next glows (the Add block button, the Math entry, the two pins to wire, the Inspector's fields, Run), the card says what to do right now and what went wrong, and Do it for me does any step. Skip any time; arrow keys move between steps |
| Git | File › Git… keeps the project in a Git repository (GitHub, GitLab, Gitea …): **Store** records what changed and sends it, **Fetch** gets what is stored and puts the two together; files both sides changed are asked about. Sign in with GitHub in the browser, or with an access token. See [Keeping a project in Git](git.md). |
| Live session | File › Live session… lets several people work in one project at once: one hosts (the project and the bot stay theirs), guests join with an invitation and may change what the host ticks for them. Sealed between the apps; the relay only passes it on. See [Live sessions](live.md). |
| Host | File › Host… pairs this computer with an XC Circuit Host (a container you run yourself), keeps a project on it, adds further devices by a code, and sends and gets a project's secrets through its vault, sealed on the devices. See [The Host](host.md). |
| Backups | Every save keeps a snapshot outside the project (newest 20, plus one a day for 14 days; Settings › Backups). File › Restore from backup… compares them with now and restores the project or one workspace. Unsaved changes are copied every 30 s (Settings › Backups › Crash recovery) and offered back after a crash |
| Bot data backups | A bot backs up its saved data (store.json) when it starts and every 6 hours, keeping the newest 10 in data/backups. If the data is empty or damaged it asks: restore a backup or start empty (a dialog in XC Circuit, a question in the terminal) |
| Shortcuts | Settings › Shortcuts: click a shortcut and press the keys you want: any key (letters, digits, F1–F24, arrows, punctuation, Home, Insert …) with any mix of Ctrl, Shift and Alt, or the mouse's side buttons. Each action can have two; a shortcut taken from another action says so. Besides Run (F5) and Stop (Shift+F5), Start and Restart alone, Bot settings, Slash Commands, Export, Upload to the server, Server console, Server settings and switching Run between this computer and the server can get one (they have none to start with); menus and the command palette show them. Shortcuts without Ctrl or Alt don't fire while typing. Copy, cut and paste stay the system's keys |
| Settings | Ctrl+, or the gear at the bottom of the activity bar: theme, accent color (changes live), touch mode, interface size, canvas, window, the Console's font, size and line spacing (any font installed on the computer; monospaced ones first, with a search), bot, plugins, shortcuts |
| Language | English and German come with the app: pick one on the first start page or in Settings › Appearance; it switches right away. Blocks (their names, descriptions and fields) stay in English |
| Touch mode | Settings › Appearance (or the first start's Look step): bigger buttons, rows and pins with more room between them, for touch screens and pens |
| Command palette | Ctrl+P or the search box in the title bar: run any command, open a workspace, or jump to a block |
| Editor tabs | Every tab shows an icon before its name. The Embed Builder, Layout Builder, Modal Builder, Slash Commands, Bot settings and Export open as tabs in their own floating window, which moves by the empty part of its tab bar and resizes at any edge or corner; drag a tab onto any side or next to other tabs to dock it, or out of every area to give it a window again. A line or a lit area shows where it goes. Closing the tab cancels it |
| Title bar | Drag to move, double-click to maximize, drag the window edges to resize; View › Use system title bar switches to the system one |
| Save | Ctrl+S (restarts a running bot) |
| Console | Every line with its time and level. Chips show one level: Info, Done, Warnings, Errors, and MCP (what AI agents did) once there is some. The Filter box keeps only lines with its text; Clear empties the Console. Show block jumps to the block that wrote a line |
| Panels | The Inspector, Console and Problems are tabs: drag them to dock anywhere, or onto the activity bar. Right-click a tab › Close or Move to the activity bar; middle-click closes it. Drag the line between two areas to resize them. Reopen closed ones from View › Panels |
| Builder windows | The Embed, Layout, Modal and Canvas Builders, Slash Commands, Bot settings and the other editors open where their window was the last time and as big (moved inside XC Circuit's window when that got smaller) |
| Older computers | Settings › Window › **Lighter drawing**: tick what to leave out, or All: No shadows, No fading, Still glows (no 30-times-a-second redrawing for them) and Simpler edges (about half the triangles); all of them when the app draws without a graphics card, unless that's unticked. **Graphics**: Automatic, OpenGL or Older OpenGL from the next start, for graphics chips that can't do DirectX 12 or Vulkan. Settings › Editor › **Save layout and settings after**: how long after the last change the app saves its layout and settings (5 s to start with; each change in the meantime starts the wait again, and it always saves when it closes) |
| Freezes | When XC Circuit stops answering for three seconds or more (Windows: "Not Responding"; a window that only isn't drawing, while it's moved or minimized, doesn't count), the Console says for how long and where it was stuck, and `freezes.log` in the app's data folder keeps the last 200 such lines. Before the first freeze of a start, it also says how the app draws (and whether in software), whether it's the x86_64 or ARM build and, on Windows, the processor. A freeze the app never came back from (closed while it hung) is said in the Console at the next start. After ten seconds stuck, Windows keeps a dump of exactly where it hangs in the `freezes` folder next to the log (the last three, a few MB each). Send the log, and the newest dump, along when you report a freeze |
| Windows of their own | Drag a tab outside XC Circuit's window and let go, or right-click it › Open in its own window: it gets a window of its own, to put on a second monitor. It looks like XC Circuit's window: drag its tab bar (or a tab) to move it, double-click it to maximize, and its edges to resize; **Back into the app** at the top right (or closing it) brings the tab back into XC Circuit's window, nothing lost. With Settings › Use system title bar it has the system's frame instead. Shortcuts with Ctrl, Alt or a function key (Ctrl+S, F5 …) work there too |
| Workspaces | The Workspaces panel lists them in folders: + and the folder button on the project row add them, drag a workspace onto a folder to move it, double-click a name to rename. Ctrl-click workspaces to select several (Ctrl-click again to take one out), or Shift-click to select all from the last one clicked; **Delete** then asks before deleting them, and so does Delete N workspaces in the menu of a selected one. Clicking elsewhere (or Escape) lets go of the selection, so Delete deletes blocks again. On the right of each: a warning sign and number for its problems, a green dot while its blocks run (red after one failed), and **off** when it's turned off; folders show how many workspaces they hold (and, closed, their problems). Hover a workspace for its blocks, events, problems and when it last ran. The ⋯ button (or right-click) has Open, Rename, **Duplicate** (a copy with all its blocks, turned off so it doesn't answer twice), Turn off/on, Move to, Export and Delete. **Turn off** leaves a workspace out of the bot (its events don't fire, its blocks don't run) without deleting it |
| Snap and arrange | The magnet in the canvas toolbar (or Settings › Canvas) snaps dropped blocks and notes to the grid. With several blocks selected, Arrange above them aligns their edges or centres, or spreads them out evenly |
| Run times and values | While the bot runs from the editor, each block shows how long it took above its corner for 30 seconds, and hovering a wire shows the last value that went through it |
| Favourite blocks | Star a block in the picker (on its row or in its details): favourites and the blocks you placed lately are listed at the top |
| Notes | Add note in the canvas toolbar, or select blocks › Note to frame them: a title, a description and a colour (pencil button or double-click the title; a preset, or Other color for any colour; the boxes grow by their corner grip). Drag the title to move the note; with its "Move blocks with the note" switch on (off for new notes), the blocks inside move along. Alt does the opposite for one drag; drag its edges or corners to resize it. Zoomed out, a note's title and description stay readable, like a map's labels (the description only while it fits in half the note). Notes don't run |
| Try Zone | Select a block › Try Zone; drop blocks in or out; the gear on the zone's title sets retries and timeout |
| Embeds | Select a Build Embed block › Open Embed Builder; the block shows a live preview. Every part of an embed is there: author with link and icon, title link, fields, images, footer, and a timestamp (when it's sent, or a set time) |
| Pictures | Select a Build Canvas block › Edit canvas…: the Canvas Builder. Start from a Rank, Welcome or Profile card; add shapes, circles, pictures, texts and bars; click to choose a layer, drag to move it, drag its corner to resize it (Shift keeps its shape), arrow keys to nudge it. Preview values show `${…}` with a value. The block shows the picture ([Pictures with Build Canvas](./canvas)) |
| Forms (modals) | Show Modal's form is designed in the Modal Builder (Edit form… on the block, or Open Modal Builder in the Inspector): a title, a custom id (what Modal Submitted matches) and up to 5 parts: questions, each with a hint and a box to type into (one line or several), a select menu (options you list, users, roles or channels) or a file upload, and texts with markdown. A preview shows it as Discord will. Modal Submitted (with the form's custom id) gives each answer as an output of its own, of its kind, by itself: a box's text, the values picked from a menu of options, the members, roles or channels picked from such a menu (as lists), the files of an upload. Its Input ids is only for forms made from blocks; ids listed there give text. The JSON view takes a modal pasted from the Discord docs. Forms made from Text Input, Form Field, File Upload and Form Text blocks wired into Show Modal's Inputs keep working; those blocks are no longer in the picker |
| Picking channels and roles | With a bot token saved, fields for a channel, category or role id (and Find Role, Find Channel, Add Role, Has Role) have a small button after the box: it lists your bot's servers with their channels (of the right kind) or roles, and puts the id of the one you pick in. Its tooltip names the one chosen. No more copying ids with Developer Mode |
| Custom ids | Button Pressed, Select Menu Used and Modal Submitted offer the custom ids your layouts, forms and Button / Select Menu blocks use (Custom… types any other, such as one made while the bot runs). Problems says when an event waits for an id nothing has (often a typo) and when a button, menu or form has no event to handle it |
| Discord's limits | The Embed, Layout, Modal and Slash Command Builders check what Discord would refuse, with its own limits: an embed's title (256 characters), description (4096), fields (25, names 256, values 1024), footer (2048), author (256) and 6000 in all; a button's label (80) and link (512, starting with https://); a select menu's placeholder (150), how many can be picked (up to 25) and its options (labels, values and descriptions up to 100, values each their own); pictures' descriptions (1024); a form's boxes (placeholder 100, filled-in text 4000) and file uploads (up to 10 files and 10 file types); a command's required options before optional ones, each option name once, up to 25 subcommands and 8000 characters in all. What a `${…}` becomes isn't counted, as it's only known when the bot runs. The builder lists them above its form, and blocks with such a design show them in Problems |
| Components V2 | A Build Layout block designs a whole message from Discord's components: containers with an accent color, text (markdown), sections with a picture or button next to the text, media galleries, files, separators, rows of buttons (every style, emoji, link and premium) and select menus (options, users, roles, channels). Edit layout… opens the Layout Builder with a Discord preview; set Send Message's Format to Layout and connect the block. Pictures and files given as file paths are attached when sending |
| JSON | The Embed Builder, Layout Builder, Modal Builder and Slash Commands each switch between Builder and JSON. The JSON is Discord's own: edit it or paste JSON from the Discord docs, discord.js `toJSON()` or a message designer, and it applies as soon as it is valid (errors show the line and column) |
| Slash commands | Bot › Slash Commands…: options with choices (a name and a value each), length and number limits, channel kinds and autocomplete; subcommands and groups; translations of every name and description into Discord's languages; the permissions people need (any number), where the command works (servers, DMs with the bot, other DMs), how the bot is installed (server or account) and age-restricted. Registered when the bot starts, and checked against Discord at every start. In the side bar, under Slash commands: click one to edit it, drag them into order or into folders (the folder button makes one; folders go in folders, as for workspaces), and turn one off (right-click) so it isn't registered |
| Databases | Bot › Settings › Databases: connections to MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite or MongoDB, each with Test connection; the default database; where stored values are kept. The blocks Get Rows, Insert Row, Update Rows, Delete Rows and SQL Query use them ([Databases](./databases)) |
| Stored data | Stored Data (the database icon in the activity bar) shows what `ctx.store` saved: add, change or delete values (read-only while the bot runs). Pick a database at the top to see its tables as a grid: page through the rows, double-click a cell to change it, Change and Delete in front of each row, Add row |
| Plugins | The Plugins view of the side bar: every plugin and how it runs, Install…, Reload, Open folder. A switch turns a plugin off or on; the trash can removes it (after asking). The plugins that come with the app can't be turned off or removed |
| Bot settings | Bot › Settings: pages on the left (Connection, Slash commands, Messages, Music, Privileged intents, and pages plugins add), the page on the right, Save at the bottom. A page with something required but unset shows a count in the list, one with a value that doesn't fit shows it in red |
| Bot token | Bot › Settings › Connection (kept in Windows Credential Manager / Linux Secret Service). The eye button shows what you typed, Copy copies the saved token without showing it, and values are checked as you type (a build mode's settings can set `pattern`, a regular expression, and `patternHint`; `sensitive = true` hides a text setting behind the eye button) |
| Invite your bot | Under the bot token, once one is typed or saved: pick the permissions (**What your blocks need**, made from the project's blocks and listed under it, or common bot permissions, Administrator or none), then **Open invite page** opens Discord's page for adding the bot to a server, or **Copy link** copies the link |
| Run / Stop | F5 / Shift+F5, or Run in the title bar. Running blocks glow; failures show on the block |
| Export | Bot › Export… writes a folder that runs with `node index.js` |
| Remote | Bot › Remote… uploads the bot to its server over SFTP or a Calagopus panel, by hand or after every save; only changed files are sent, and the server's `data/` is never touched. For a Calagopus server, sign in through the browser; Bot › Remote console has Start, Restart, Stop, Kill and the live console ([Putting your bot on a server](./hosting)) |

Running needs Node.js 22 or newer; the first start page (or Settings › Bot › Node.js) finds or installs it. The first run installs the mode's npm packages (discord.js, or @fluxerjs/core for Fluxer bots) once, into `%APPDATA%\XC Circuit\packages` or `~/.local/share/xc-circuit/packages`.


---

<!-- docs/plugins/recipes.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/plugins/recipes -->

# Recipes

::: info In short
Complete examples for things plugins often do. Copy one into your plugin, change the ids to your plugin's, and save: it loads right away. Blocks go into a file listed under `[contributes] blocks`; editor code goes into the `editor.js` named under `[editor]`.
:::

Each recipe says where its code goes. The ids start with `acme.`: use your plugin's id instead.

## Blocks

### A value block

Turns its input into something else; no action wires. `blocks/initials.js`:

```js
module.exports = {
  id: "acme.initials",
  kind: "value",
  info: { name: "Initials", description: "The first letter of each word, in capitals: Ada Lovelace → AL.", author: "Acme", version: "1.0.0" },
  search: { category: "text", aliases: ["Monogram"] },
  look: { icon: "text" },
  fields: { text: { type: "text", pin: true } },
  outputs: { initials: { type: "text" } },
  run({ fields }) {
    const initials = String(fields.text).split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean).map((w) => w[0].toUpperCase()).join("");
    return { initials };
  },
};
```

### An action with a choice

An action runs in a flow and continues on its action output. A `select` field gives a dropdown, and `show` hides fields that don't apply. `blocks/count.js`:

```js
module.exports = {
  id: "acme.count",
  kind: "action",
  info: { name: "Count", description: "Adds one to a counter kept for the bot or for a member, and gives the new count.", author: "Acme", version: "1.0.0" },
  search: { category: "data" },
  look: { icon: "hash" },
  fields: {
    scope: { type: "select", choices: { bot: "Whole bot", user: "Per user" }, default: "bot" },
    user: { type: "discord.user", pin: "only", show: { scope: ["user"] } },
    key: { type: "text", default: "count" },
  },
  outputs: { count: { type: "number" } },
  async run({ fields, ctx }) {
    const store = fields.scope === "user" ? ctx.store.user(fields.user.id) : ctx.store.global();
    return { count: await store.inc(fields.key) };
  },
};
```

### Branching

`flows` gives an action several ways out; [`ctx.next`](/api/ctx#next) picks one. `blocks/chance.js`:

```js
module.exports = {
  id: "acme.chance",
  kind: "action",
  info: { name: "Chance", description: "Goes on through Hit with the given chance, otherwise through Miss.", author: "Acme", version: "1.0.0" },
  search: { category: "flow", aliases: ["Random", "Probability"] },
  look: { icon: "branch" },
  fields: { percent: { type: "number", default: 50, min: 0, max: 100 } },
  flows: ["hit", "miss"],
  async run({ fields, ctx }) {
    await ctx.next(Math.random() * 100 < fields.percent ? "hit" : "miss");
  },
};
```

### Calling a web API

Use [`ctx.util.fetch`](/api/ctx#util): it limits the size of the answer and, for addresses the bot's users typed, keeps to the public web. `blocks/joke.js`:

```js
module.exports = {
  id: "acme.joke",
  kind: "action",
  info: { name: "Get Joke", description: "Gets a random joke from the web.", author: "Acme", version: "1.0.0" },
  search: { category: "web" },
  look: { icon: "message" },
  outputs: { joke: { type: "text" } },
  async run({ ctx }) {
    const { res, body } = await ctx.util.fetch("https://official-joke-api.appspot.com/random_joke", { headers: { accept: "application/json" } });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`The joke service answered ${res.status}`);
    const j = JSON.parse(body.toString("utf8"));
    return { joke: `${j.setup} ${j.punchline}` };
  },
};
```

A thrown `Error` fails the block: it turns red, and the message goes to the Console (or to a [Try Zone](/explanations/errors)).

### An npm package

List it under `requires.dependencies`; XC Circuit installs it before Run and puts it into exports. Load it with [`ctx.require`](/api/ctx#require). `blocks/slug.js`:

```js
module.exports = {
  id: "acme.slug",
  kind: "value",
  info: { name: "Slug", description: "A text as a web-address-friendly slug: Hello World! → hello-world.", author: "Acme", version: "1.0.0" },
  search: { category: "text" },
  requires: { dependencies: { slugify: "^1.6.6" } },
  fields: { text: { type: "text", pin: true } },
  outputs: { slug: { type: "text" } },
  run({ fields, ctx }) {
    const slugify = ctx.require("slugify");
    return { slug: slugify(String(fields.text), { lower: true, strict: true }) };
  },
};
```

### Keeping data apart

Stored data your blocks keep can go into a namespace of your own, so it can't clash with the bot's own keys: [`ctx.store.ns`](/api/ctx#store).

```js
const seen = ctx.store.ns("acme.tools");
await seen.set(`last:${fields.user.id}`, Date.now());
```

It shows in Stored Data under `ns:acme.tools`.

## The editor

### A command

In the Plugins menu and the command palette (Ctrl+P). `editor.js`:

```js
xc.command({
  id: "acme.count-logs",
  title: "Count Log blocks",
  run() {
    const logs = xc.blocks().filter((b) => b.type === "core.log");
    xc.success(`${logs.length} Log blocks in ${xc.project().name}`);
  },
});
```

### A check for the Problems panel

Runs about once a second. A problem that names a block selects it when clicked.

```js
xc.check(() =>
  xc.blocks()
    .filter((b) => b.type === "core.log" && !b.values.message)
    .map((b) => ({ message: "This Log has no message", workspace: b.workspace, block: b.id })),
);
```

### A panel that lists and jumps

`render` runs again when the project changes, so it's always current.

```js
xc.panel({
  id: "acme.todo",
  title: "TODO notes",
  render(ui) {
    const todos = xc.workspaces().flatMap((w) =>
      Object.values(xc.workspace(w.key).notes ?? {})
        .filter((n) => /TODO/i.test(n.text ?? ""))
        .map((n) => ({ workspace: w, note: n })),
    );
    if (!todos.length) return ui.muted("No notes with TODO.");
    for (const t of todos) {
      ui.row((ui) => {
        ui.text(t.workspace.name, { bold: true });
        ui.text(t.note.text);
      });
    }
  },
});
```

### Settings for your plugin

Panels are *controlled*: keep what people type and give it back on the next render. [`xc.storage`](/api/editor#quick-reference) keeps it on this computer, between sessions.

```js
xc.panel({
  id: "acme.settings",
  title: "Acme settings",
  render(ui) {
    const s = xc.storage.get("settings") ?? { greeting: "Hello", loud: false };
    const save = (change) => xc.storage.set("settings", { ...s, ...change });
    ui.input(s.greeting, (greeting) => save({ greeting }), { placeholder: "Greeting", key: "greeting" });
    ui.toggle("Shout it", s.loud, (loud) => save({ loud }));
    ui.button("Try it", () => xc.log(s.loud ? s.greeting.toUpperCase() + "!" : s.greeting), { primary: true });
  },
});
```

For settings that belong to the project (and go with it to other computers), use `xc.data` with a key starting with your plugin's id.

### Adding blocks for someone

Changes go through undo like the person's own edits.

```js
xc.command({
  id: "acme.add-log",
  title: "Add a Log next to the selection",
  run() {
    const ws = xc.activeWorkspace();
    const [first] = xc.selection();
    if (!ws || !first) return xc.warn("Select a block first.");
    const at = xc.workspace(ws).nodes[first].at ?? [0, 0];
    const id = xc.addBlock(ws, "core.log", { x: at[0] + 260, y: at[1], values: { message: "Here!" } });
    xc.select(ws, [id]);
  },
});
```

### Reacting to the running bot

`xc.on("botEvent")` gets what the bot run from the editor does: starts, stops, logs, and every block that runs (keep that quick).

```js
let failed = 0;
xc.on("botEvent", (e) => {
  if (e.type === "started") failed = 0;
  if (e.type === "block" && e.error) failed += 1;
});
xc.panel({
  id: "acme.health",
  title: "Bot health",
  render(ui) {
    ui.stat("failed blocks since start", failed);
    ui.button(xc.botRunning() ? "Stop" : "Run", () => xc.run(xc.botRunning() ? "bot.stop" : "bot.run"));
  },
});
```

### Something on a timer

```js
let ticks = 0;
xc.every(60_000, () => {
  ticks += 1;
  if (ticks % 30 === 0) xc.log("Half an hour of work: time for a break?");
});
```

## More

- DemoBot's `plugins/demo.custom/`: a block, a panel, a command and a check together.
- [Desk Pet](https://github.com/XCraftTM/XC-Circuit/tree/main/examples/plugins/desk-pet): an overlay with pictures, sounds and timers.
- The bundled plugins in the app's `plugins/` folder: every block XC Circuit has, as ordinary plugin files.


---

<!-- docs/plugins/share.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/plugins/share -->

# Share and update

::: info In short
Raise `version` in `plugin.toml` for every change, zip the plugin folder, and share the zip: people install it with Plugins › Install from Zip… (or by dropping it on the window). Of two copies of a plugin, the higher version loads. Never change a block's `id`; raise its own major version and add `migrate` when its saved values change.
:::

## Before you share

- [ ] `id` is yours and every block and command id starts with it.
- [ ] `name`, `author`, `description` and `version` are filled in: the Plugins view shows them.
- [ ] `[engines] circuit = "^1.0"`, and `app = "…"` if your blocks need something only newer XC Circuit versions have.
- [ ] `[dependencies]` names the plugins yours needs (`"xc.discord" = "^1.0"` for Discord blocks).
- [ ] Every block has `info.name`, `info.description`, `info.author` and `info.version`, and a `search.category`.
- [ ] Nothing in the folder you don't want to give away: no `.env`, tokens, test data or `node_modules`.
- [ ] It loads without problems on a fresh project: the Problems panel is empty.

## Make the zip

Zip the plugin **folder** (so `plugin.toml` is in one folder at the top of the zip) or its **contents** (`plugin.toml` at the top). Both install. GitHub's *Code › Download ZIP* of a repository that is one plugin works too.

```
acme.tools-1.2.0.zip
└─ acme.tools/
   ├─ plugin.toml
   ├─ blocks/…
   └─ editor.js
```

## Installing

**Plugins › Install from Zip…**, the **Install…** button in the Plugins view, or dropping the `.zip` on the window. It goes into your plugins folder and loads right away; the Console says what was installed.

A plugin can also come with a project: one in the project's `plugins/` folder loads whenever the project is open, and goes along when the project is copied or shared. That's the way for a plugin made for one bot.

## Turning off and removing

In the **Plugins view** of the side bar (the plug icon), each plugin you installed has a switch and a trash can:

- **The switch** turns the plugin off: its blocks, panels, commands and themes are gone until you turn it on again. It stays listed. A project that uses its blocks needs it turned on again to work as before.
- **The trash can** removes it: after you confirm, its folder is deleted.

The plugins that come with XC Circuit (Circuit Core, Discord Bot, Fluxer Bot, Server Tools) say *Built in* and can't be turned off or removed.

## Versions

`version` is `major.minor.patch`. Raise it **for every change you share**:

| Change | Raise | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a fix | patch | 1.2.0 → 1.2.1 |
| something new (a block, a panel, a field with a default) | minor | 1.2.1 → 1.3.0 |
| something that breaks what people built | major | 1.3.0 → 2.0.0 |

**Updating is installing the newer zip.** When the same plugin (`id`) is in two places, the higher `version` loads, so a newer copy in the plugins folder wins over an older one in a project, and the other way round.

### Changing a block that's in use

Projects save each block by its `id` and its own **major** version (`acme.count@1`), with the values filled in:

- **Never change a block's `id`**: projects that use it would show it as unknown.
- Adding a field with a `default`, a new output or a better description: no new major version needed.
- Renaming or removing a field, or changing what a value means: raise the block's `info.version` major (`1.4.0` → `2.0.0`) and add [`migrate`](/api/blocks#migrate), which turns old saved values into new ones when a project opens.
- A block you want to retire: `info.deprecated: "Use Count instead"`. It keeps working, but the picker hides it.

### Needing a newer XC Circuit

If your blocks use something new in XC Circuit (a `ctx` member, a field type), set `[engines] app` to the version that has it. Older versions then don't load your plugin, instead of failing while the bot runs.

## Publishing a plugin's code

A Git repository whose top folder is the plugin is the easiest to share: people download the zip from GitHub, and you develop it with [`XC_CIRCUIT_PLUGINS`](./#where-to-keep-it-while-you-work) pointing at the folder above it. Put a `README.md` in the folder; XC Circuit ignores files it doesn't know.


---

<!-- docs/api/blocks.md · https://xcrafttm.github.io/XC-Circuit/api/blocks -->

# Blocks

::: info In short
A block is one JavaScript or TypeScript file that exports an object: an `id`, a `kind` (`"event"`, `"action"` or `"value"`), `info` (name, description…), `fields` (what you fill in), `outputs` (what it gives) and `run()` (what it does).
:::

A block is one `.js`, `.cjs`, `.mjs` or `.ts` file that exports an object. Files are found through the plugin's `contributes.blocks` patterns.

```js
module.exports = {
  id: "acme.shout",
  kind: "value",
  info: { name: "Shout", description: "Upper-cases a text.", author: "Acme", version: "1.0.0" },
  search: { category: "text", aliases: ["Uppercase"] },
  look: { icon: "text" },
  fields: { text: { type: "text", pin: true } },
  outputs: { result: { type: "text" } },
  run({ fields }) {
    return { result: String(fields.text).toUpperCase() + "!" };
  },
};
```

`export default { … }` works too, and so do TypeScript files: XC Circuit strips the types when it loads them (it doesn't check them; your code editor does, with [`@xc-circuit/sdk`](#typescript)).

## Keys

| Key | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | text | **Required.** Unique id, starting with your plugin's id: `acme.shout`. Never change it once people use the block: projects refer to blocks by id. |
| `kind` | `"event"` · `"action"` · `"value"` | **Required.** See [Events, actions and values](/explanations/blocks-and-wires). |
| `info` | object | What the block is. [Below](#info). |
| `search` | object | How the block picker finds it. [Below](#search). |
| `look` | object | How it looks. [Below](#look). |
| `requires` | object | What it needs to run. [Below](#requires). |
| `fields` | object | Inputs filled in on the block (or connected), by key. See [Fields and types](./fields). |
| `outputs` | object | Values it gives, by key: `{ type, label?, description? }`. |
| `flows` | list of text | Action outputs of an action with more than one way out. [Below](#flows). |
| `pure` | boolean | Value blocks only. By default a value block runs once per run and its outputs are reused; `pure: false` runs it again every time a value is needed (for random numbers, the current time…). |
| `run` | function | What the block does. [Below](#run). |
| `listen` | function | Events only: subscribes to what starts a flow. [Below](#listen). |
| `setup` | function | Runs once when the bot starts, before events subscribe. |
| `define` | function | Runs in the **editor** to change fields and outputs from the block's values and connections. [Below](#define). |
| `migrate` | function | Upgrades saved values when the major version changes. [Below](#migrate). |

The keys inside `info`, `search`, `look` and `requires` may also stand at the top level (older block files do this); a key given in both places is reported.

### info

| Key | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | **Required.** The block's name, in English, in Title Case: *Send Message*. |
| `description` | **Required.** One or two sentences: what it does, for someone who hasn't used it. |
| `author` | **Required.** Who wrote it. |
| `version` | **Required.** `major.minor.patch`. The **major** version is saved with every use of the block (`acme.shout@1`); raise it when old saved values need [`migrate`](#migrate). |
| `docs` | A web address with more help (`https://…`): the Inspector's Docs button opens it, and nothing that isn't a web address. |
| `deprecated` | `true` or a text saying what to use instead. The block stays usable, but the picker hides it. |

### search

| Key | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `category` | A category id of the build mode, such as `send`, `members`, `text` or `flow` (see [Build modes](./build-modes#categories)). Events go into the category of the blocks they work with. |
| `aliases` | Other English names the picker finds the block by (*Reply* for Send Message). They rank like the name and are never shown. |
| `tags` | More search words, ranked after the name and aliases. |

### look

| Key | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `icon` | An icon name from any plugin's `icons`: `message`, `user`, `clock`, `hash`, `branch`… |
| `width` | The block's width on the canvas, in points. |
